docs.title: boti-data
docs.text:
boti-data is the data access and data transformation layer of the Boti ecosystem.

It builds on top of boti and gives teams a reusable interface for working with structured data across databases, parquet datasets, schema-controlled transformations, and distributed or partitioned loading workflows.

docs.title: What boti-data is for
docs.text:
Many teams have the same recurring problem: business logic depends on data that lives in multiple places, arrives in slightly different shapes, and is loaded through a mix of notebooks, scripts, ad hoc SQL, and one-off helpers.

boti-data helps turn that into a more coherent data access layer.

It is designed for codebases that need to:

  • connect to named data sources consistently
  • reflect or model database tables without hand-writing everything up front
  • load data through a gateway instead of bespoke query snippets everywhere
  • normalise and validate schemas before downstream use
  • combine parquet and database workflows in one library
  • scale from simple local reads to partitioned or distributed loading

docs.title: Problems boti-data solves
docs.text:
boti-data is useful when data code is suffering from issues like:

  • repeated connection boilerplate across notebooks and services
  • slow, fragile query code copied from place to place
  • inconsistent schema assumptions between producers and consumers
  • difficult transitions from exploratory analysis to reusable pipelines
  • manual join and field-mapping logic repeated in many modules
  • no common abstraction for loading data from SQL and parquet sources

By centralising those patterns, boti-data reduces duplicated plumbing and makes transformations easier to reason about.

docs.title: Why boti-data can make a huge difference
docs.text:
The biggest benefit of boti-data is that it creates a shared data interface between infrastructure and business logic.

That means teams can spend less time rewriting access code and more time working on actual transformations, validation rules, and downstream decisions.

It can make a major difference when:

  • analysts and engineers share the same source systems
  • a notebook prototype needs to become production code
  • multiple data products depend on the same tables or parquet layouts
  • schema drift is a recurring source of errors
  • large extracts need partitioning or distributed execution
  • teams want a clean boundary between connection details and transformation logic

docs.title: Domain areas where it is especially valuable
docs.text:
boti-data is intentionally general-purpose, but it is especially strong in domains where structured operational data must be transformed into reliable analytical or decision-ready datasets.

Examples include:

  • analytics engineering: building reusable source loaders, schema maps, and standardised transformations
  • business operations: consolidating data from transactional systems, planning tools, and operational databases
  • finance and controlling: reconciling structured data with explicit schema expectations and repeatable joins
  • risk, compliance, and audit: validating input shape, tracing transformations, and standardising access patterns
  • customer and product analytics: joining behavioural and operational datasets with less custom plumbing
  • supply chain and logistics: unifying inventory, movement, order, and status data from several systems
  • data platform and internal tooling: giving teams a common gateway layer instead of ad hoc connectors
  • ML feature preparation: building reliable dataset assembly steps from SQL and parquet sources

In those settings, the gains are not just convenience. They show up as better reuse, fewer integration bugs, and faster movement from exploration to production.

docs.title: Big-data readiness
docs.text: Boti is ready for Dask-first large workloads today, with some clear boundaries.

docs.title: Recommended operating model
docs.text:
1. Use return_type="dask" for large reads.
  2. Run under an explicit Dask client or dask_session(...).
  3. Prefer partitioned SQL reads or parquet-backed datasets.
  4. Prune columns and push filters down as early as possible.
  5. Use indexed_left_join(...) for large distributed joins after aligning join-key dtypes.
  6. Persist after expensive repartition/index boundaries when the result will be reused.
  7. Materialize only at the edge for exports, samples, or compact aggregates.
  8. Use resilient=True when you want Dask persistence to go through the resilience layer.
  9. Use apply_recommended_dask_config(...) for shuffle-heavy workloads.

docs.title: What Boti already supports
docs.text:
• partitioned SQL loading through DataGateway and SqlPartitionedLoader
  • lazy Dask execution on local or external distributed schedulers
  • explicit session ownership via DaskSession / dask_session(...)
  • schema-aware distributed joins via indexed_left_join(...)
  • resilient Dask helpers for sync, async, and distributed actions
  • opt-in resilient indexed joins via indexed_left_join(..., resilient=True)
  • opt-in Dask config preset via apply_recommended_dask_config(...)
  • opt-in diagnostics on gateway loads and joins with diagnostics=True
  • eager result modes (pandas, arrow, polars) for small-result convenience

docs.title: What diagnostics=True gives you
docs.text:
For gateway loads:

  • requested vs resolved return type
  • active Dask client summary
  • partition plan summary
  • load timing and Dask graph/partition metrics

For joins:

  • active client summary
  • input/output frame metrics
  • timing for indexed joins
  • warning when a direct Dask merge is likely to trigger a large shuffle
  • warning when persist=False may cause repeated recomputation
  • graph metrics for lazy Dask gateway loads

docs.title: SQL-backed workloads
docs.text:
• Prefer file-backed or network-reachable databases for worker access.
  • Keep partitioned statements free of LIMIT, OFFSET, and ORDER BY; let the loader manage partition planning.
  • Choose explicit partition_column / order_column when defaults are not ideal.

docs.title: Parquet-backed workloads
docs.text:
• Prefer parquet for repeated large analytics and intermediate datasets.
  • Organize data so partition pruning is meaningful.
  • Use filesystem profiles or project-rooted paths that are visible to the workers.

docs.title: Join-heavy workloads
docs.text:
• Normalize join-key dtypes before joining.
  • For large joins, set indexes on the join key and join on the index.
  • Persist after set_index(...) if downstream work will reuse the result.
  • Prefer resilient=True for long-running or remote distributed joins.

docs.title: Readiness status
docs.text:
Ready now

  • local distributed development
  • explicit remote-style scheduler attachment
  • partitioned SQL + parquet lazy loading
  • indexed distributed joins
  • basic diagnostics and workload visibility
  • resilience helpers for compute/persist/wait/inspection
  • recommended opt-in config profile for shuffle-heavy jobs

Still maturing

  • broader validation against real remote clusters and object stores
  • heavier benchmark coverage for skew, spill, and failure scenarios
  • more production cookbook material for deployment-specific tuning

docs.title: Minimal example
docs.text:
from dask.distributed import LocalCluster
from sqlalchemy import select

from boti_data import (
    DataGateway,
    SqlDatabaseConfig,
    apply_recommended_dask_config,
    dask_session,
    indexed_left_join,
)

config = SqlDatabaseConfig(connection_url="sqlite:///warehouse.db", query_only=False)

with apply_recommended_dask_config():
    with LocalCluster(n_workers=2, threads_per_worker=1, processes=False, dashboard_address=":0") as cluster:
        with dask_session(scheduler_address=cluster.scheduler_address):
            with DataGateway(config) as gateway:
                left = gateway.load(
                    statement=select(User),
                    model=User,
                    persist=True,
                    resilient=True,
                    diagnostics=True,
                )
                right = gateway.load(
                    statement=select(UserProfile),
                    model=UserProfile,
                    persist=True,
                    resilient=True,
                    diagnostics=True,
                )
                joined = indexed_left_join(
                    left,
                    right,
                    join_key="id",
                    join_schema_map={"id": "Int64"},
                    persist=True,
                    resilient=True,
                    diagnostics=True,
                )
                result = joined.head()

docs.title: Dask resilience and cluster-lifecycle use cases for boti-data
Summary
docs.text:
Reviewing sibi_flux.dask_cluster and sibi_dst.utils.dask_resilience shows a consistent theme: both packages add a resilience layer above ordinary Dask usage rather than replacing Dask itself. The main ideas are:

  • keep a healthy client available
  • retry on recoverable comm failures
  • avoid unsafe fallback for Dask DataFrame graphs
  • expose graph and cluster diagnostics
  • optionally share or heal cluster state across processes

boti-data now relies on boti_dask for this runtime foundation:

  • ../boti-dask/src/boti_dask/session.py for explicit client/session ownership
  • ../boti-dask/src/boti_dask/resilience.py for resilient wrappers and emptiness helpers
  • ../boti-dask/src/boti_dask/diagnostics.py for graph/frame diagnostics
  • src/boti_data/gateway/core.py for load diagnostics and client summaries
  • src/boti_data/joins.py for diagnostics around large distributed joins
  • src/boti_data/db/partitioned_loader.py for worker-safe partitioned SQL loading

That means the best opportunity is selective adoption: add resilience and observability around high-value distributed operations without importing the full lifecycle model from the reviewed projects.

docs.text:

  • registry/watchdog lifecycle management
  • worker code deployment

docs.title: sibi_flux.dask_cluster
docs.text:
Most relevant patterns:

  • persistent/shared client registry via a temp-file registry and refcounting
  • connectivity verification before accepting a scheduler/client as healthy
  • watchdog-based healing when scheduler comms fail
  • safe compute/persist/gather wrappers with one retry after client rebind
  • strict invariant: never silently fall back to local threaded compute for Dask DataFrame/Series graphs
  • graph inspection / dry run to log task count, layers, and partition counts before execution
  • optional local code deployment to workers for remote scheduler scenarios

This module is the stronger reference for cluster lifecycle and operational safety.

docs.title: sibi_dst.utils.dask_resilience
docs.text:
Most relevant patterns:

  • global Dask config hardening, especially dataframe.shuffle.method = "tasks"
  • narrower recoverable exception policy
  • sync and async safe wrappers for compute/persist/gather/wait
  • cheap emptiness probes for Dask collections
  • resilient unique value extraction

This module is the stronger reference for execution wrappers and defensive data utilities.

docs.title: Current boti-data baseline
docs.text:
boti-data already supports (directly or through boti_dask):

  • explicit DaskSession / dask_session(...)
  • local or remote scheduler attachment
  • diagnostics for gateway loads and joins
  • partitioned SQL execution designed for worker-local engines
  • Dask-first joins through indexed_left_join(...)

What it does not currently provide:

  • automatic client healing or rebind-and-retry
  • resilient wrappers around expensive distributed actions
  • persistent shared-cluster reuse across notebook/process boundaries
  • explicit dry-run graph inspection before large actions
  • Dask-specific helpers like resilient emptiness/unique-value probes

docs.title: 1. Resilient materialization of expensive Dask loads
Problem
docs.text:
Large DataGateway.load(..., return_type="dask") workloads often end in a small number of materialization points:

  • .persist() after repartition or indexing
  • .compute() for exports or model inputs
  • .head() / sample extraction for notebook inspection

If the client drops during these steps, users currently have to manage recovery themselves.

docs.title: Use case
docs.text:
Add opt-in helpers such as:

  • safe_compute(frame, client=None, logger=None)
  • safe_persist(frame, client=None, logger=None)
  • safe_wait(obj, client=None, timeout=None)

These should:

  1. detect an active client
  2. retry once on recoverable comm failures
  3. refuse unsafe local fallback for Dask DataFrames
  4. surface a clear error instructing the caller to rebuild the collection when the graph is orphaned

docs.title: Likely touchpoints
docs.text:
• ../boti-dask/src/boti_dask/resilience.py
  • src/boti_data/gateway/core.py
  • src/boti_data/joins.py

docs.title: Value
docs.text: High. This directly protects the most expensive user-visible operations in boti-data.

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: indexed_left_join(...) already recommends persist=True for expensive join pipelines, but the actual persist step is still a plain Dask action. If a cluster hiccup happens after set_index(...), the user may face recomputation or ambiguous failures.

docs.title: Use case
docs.text:
Wrap the expensive boundary operations used by distributed joins:

  • optional resilient persist after set_index(...)
  • resilient persist on the final joined frame
  • clearer diagnostics when a join graph becomes invalid after cluster recreation

docs.title: Likely touchpoints
docs.text: • src/boti_data/joins.py

docs.title: Value
docs.text: High. Join-heavy workflows are one of the clearest “big data” use cases in this repo.

docs.title: 3. Dry-run graph inspection for large distributed operations
Problem
docs.text: boti-data already logs frame summaries after work is planned or completed, but it does not provide a first-class way to inspect graph size before execution.

docs.title: Use case
docs.text:
Add an optional dry-run / inspection helper for Dask-backed frames that logs:

  • task count
  • number of partitions
  • number of graph layers
  • active client summary

This could be used in:

  • DataGateway.load(..., diagnostics=True, dry_run=True) for distributed loads
  • indexed_left_join(..., diagnostics=True, dry_run=True) before a large shuffle/index stage

docs.title: Likely touchpoints
docs.text:
• ../boti-dask/src/boti_dask/diagnostics.py
  • src/boti_data/gateway/core.py
  • src/boti_data/joins.py

docs.title: Value
docs.text: Medium-high. This would improve notebook ergonomics and preflight checks for production jobs.

docs.title: 4. Shared cluster/session reuse in notebook and ETL workflows
Problem
docs.text: boti-data has explicit session ownership, which is clean and predictable, but repeated notebook cells or multi-step ETL scripts may repeatedly reconnect or recreate clients.

docs.title: Use case
docs.text:
Introduce an optional shared-session mode on top of DaskSession, for example:

  • reuse the current context client if one exists
  • otherwise attach to a configured scheduler address
  • optionally keep a process-local singleton client for repeated operations

This does not require the full file-registry model from sibi_flux on day one.

docs.title: Likely touchpoints
docs.text:
• ../boti-dask/src/boti_dask/session.py
  • src/boti_data/helper.py

docs.title: Value
docs.text: Medium. Good fit for notebook-heavy and service-like workloads, but should remain opt-in.

docs.title: 5. Defensive Dask defaults for shuffle-heavy pipelines
Problem
docs.text: The reviewed modules explicitly harden Dask config for comm timeouts, memory spill thresholds, and shuffle behavior. boti-data currently leaves these concerns largely to caller environment and cluster configuration.

docs.title: Use case
docs.text:
Provide a documented or opt-in config profile for large distributed boti-data workloads, especially:

  • dataframe.shuffle.method = "tasks"
  • conservative comm timeout defaults
  • memory spill / pause thresholds
  • large-graph warning thresholds

This is especially relevant for:

  • indexed_left_join(...)
  • partitioned SQL loads feeding downstream joins
  • large parquet scans followed by repartition or groupby

docs.title: Likely touchpoints
docs.text:
• ../boti-dask/src/boti_dask/resilience.py
  • docs and example notebooks

docs.title: Value
docs.text: Medium-high. Likely the simplest way to reduce operational failures without invasive code changes.

docs.title: Problem
docs.text:
Big Dask frames are often probed for:

  • “is this empty?”
  • “give me representative unique values”
  • “can I cheaply inspect a few results before computing all of it?”

Naive implementations can be either too expensive or fragile.

docs.title: Use case
docs.text:
Add small utilities such as:

  • dask_is_probably_empty(frame)
  • dask_is_empty(frame, sample=4, client=None)
  • extract_unique_values(frame, *columns, limit=...)

These would be useful in:

  • UI/data validation layers built on top of DataHelper
  • diagnostics notebooks
  • data quality checks before exporting or joining

docs.title: Likely touchpoints
docs.text: • ../boti-dask/src/boti_dask/resilience.py

docs.title: Value
docs.text: Medium. Useful, but secondary to resilient compute/persist/wait.

docs.title: 7. Remote-cluster bootstrap and worker code deployment
Problem
docs.text: sibi_flux includes automatic package zip/upload to workers and registry-driven cluster healing. That is useful when workers do not automatically have the same Python package available.

docs.title: Use case in boti-data
docs.text: Limited. boti-data is primarily a library, and worker environment packaging is usually better solved through deployment tooling, container images, or environment management rather than runtime zip upload.

docs.title: Value
docs.text: Low for near-term adoption. This is probably not the first place to invest.

docs.title: Recommended adoption order
docs.text: Priority Candidate Why it fits boti-data 1 resilient compute/persist/wait wrappers protects the most expensive distributed actions with minimal API surface 2 join-boundary resilience directly improves indexed_left_join(...) workflows 3 dry-run graph inspection complements existing diagnostics cleanly 4 opt-in Dask config profile low-cost operational improvement 5 emptiness/unique-value helpers useful utilities for notebook and validation workflows 6 shared singleton session mode helpful, but should stay optional 7 registry/watchdog + code deployment operationally heavier than current repo needs

docs.title: Prefer wrappers over automatic magic
docs.text:
The reviewed packages are comfortable with hidden healing and shared global state. boti-data currently favors more explicit control. The best fit is:

  • explicit session ownership by default
  • opt-in resilience helpers
  • strong diagnostics when healing or retry happens
  • no silent fallback from distributed DataFrame graphs to local execution

docs.title: Keep DataFrame safety as an invariant
docs.text:
One of the best ideas in both reviewed modules is the rule:

if a Dask DataFrame graph loses its client or worker dependencies, do not pretend local compute is a safe fallback.

That rule aligns well with boti-data’s big-data positioning and should be preserved if resilience helpers are added.

docs.title: Reuse existing diagnostics surface
docs.text:
boti-data already has:

  • current_client_summary()
  • describe_frame(...)
  • gateway load diagnostics
  • join diagnostics

New resilience features should plug into that existing logging model instead of creating a parallel system.

docs.title: Concrete near-term proposal
docs.text:
The first increment was implemented in boti_dask, which now provides:

  1. safe_compute
  2. safe_persist
  3. safe_wait
  4. inspect_graph
  5. an opt-in Dask config helper for large shuffles

Then wire those helpers into:

  • indexed_left_join(..., persist=True, diagnostics=True)
  • large DataGateway distributed loads when diagnostics=True
  • examples and docs for notebook / ETL usage

This would capture most of the practical value from the reviewed modules without importing the heaviest parts of their lifecycle model.

docs.title: Final assessment
docs.text:
The reviewed modules are relevant to boti-data, but not as a direct transplant.

The strongest boti-data use cases are:

  • resilient compute/persist/wait around large Dask frames
  • safer distributed join workflows
  • graph inspection before expensive execution
  • documented Dask hardening defaults for shuffle-heavy analytics

The weakest use cases are:

  • full registry-based cluster lifecycle management
  • automatic worker code deployment

In short, boti-data should borrow the execution-safety and observability ideas first, while keeping cluster ownership explicit and lightweight.

docs.title: Datacube Contract
docs.text: boti-data supports callable-backed datacube loading through DatacubeConfig. Use DatacubeContract when you want typed request hooks and centralized validation.

docs.title: Contract Hooks
docs.text:
DatacubeContract supports these optional hooks:

  • request_transformer(request) -> request
  • request_validator(request) -> None
  • loader(request) -> frame
  • async_loader(request) -> awaitable[frame]
  • frame_transformer(frame, request) -> frame

Supported frame outputs are:

  • pandas.DataFrame
  • dask.dataframe.DataFrame
  • pyarrow.Table
  • polars.DataFrame

docs.title: Execution Order
docs.text:
At runtime, DatacubeResource applies hooks in this order:

  1. apply default_cube when request has no explicit cube
  2. run request_transformer (if set)
  3. run request_validator (if set)
  4. execute loader (contract.async_loader / contract.loader first, then config loaders)
  5. run frame_transformer (if set)

Loader precedence:

  • sync path: contract.loader -> DatacubeConfig.loader
  • async path: contract.async_loader -> DatacubeConfig.async_loader -> sync fallback in thread

docs.title: Validation Failures
docs.text:
If request_validator raises, boti-data surfaces an actionable error message with request context:

  • selected cube
  • list of filter keys
  • guidance to fix validator inputs or validator logic

Example message shape:

Datacube contract request validation failed: cube must be 'orders'. Request context cube='inventory', filter_keys=['status__exact']. Adjust DatacubeContract.request_validator or pass valid cube/filter inputs.

For end-to-end SQL/datacube defensive defaults, see docs/SECURITY_HARDENING.md.

docs.title: Minimal Pattern
docs.text:
import pandas as pd

from boti_data import DatacubeConfig, DatacubeContract, DataGateway


def loader(request):
    return pd.DataFrame({"id": [1], "status": ["active"]})


def validator(request):
    if request.cube != "orders":
        raise ValueError("cube must be 'orders'")


contract = DatacubeContract(
    loader=loader,
    request_validator=validator,
    request_transformer=lambda request: request.model_copy(
        update={"cube": request.cube or "orders"}
    ),
)

with DataGateway(DatacubeConfig(contract=contract)) as gateway:
    frame = gateway.load(return_type="pandas", status__exact="active")

docs.title: Phase 1 Implementation Status
docs.text:
Implemented in src/boti_data/gateway/core.py:

  • Auto chunking now receives resolved execution mode (eager/lazy).
  • Eager SQL auto chunking is disabled for medium IN lists on SQLite.
  • Eager SQL auto chunking threshold is now dialect-aware:
  • SQLite: auto chunk only when IN >= 8,000.
  • Other SQL backends: fallback threshold 5,000.
  • Eager SQL chunk fan-out concurrency is capped to 1 when auto chunking does apply.

Unit tests added:

  • tests/data/test_facade.py::test_facade_auto_in_chunking_disables_eager_sql_for_medium_in_lists
  • tests/data/test_facade.py::test_facade_auto_in_chunking_keeps_lazy_sql_chunking_for_medium_in_lists

docs.title: Observed impact vs baseline
docs.text:
• Eager auto chunking improved significantly for large IN lists:
  • sync_pandas_auto_chunk, IN=10k: 186.69 ms -> 42.50 ms (~4.4x faster).

  2. For eager paths (pandas/polars):

  5. SQLite baseline suggestion: do not auto-chunk until at least IN >= 8,000.
  6. Cap eager chunk concurrency at 1 by default:
  7. Avoid thread fan-out overhead for local DB workloads.

  2. backend-native array strategies (where supported)

docs.title: PyArrow Integration Proposal — Enhancing Boti Performance
Executive Summary
docs.text:
Boti currently uses PyArrow only for filesystem I/O and parquet dataset discovery. All in-memory data flows through pandas/Dask, missing significant performance opportunities. This proposal outlines a phased integration strategy to leverage PyArrow's zero-copy reads, vectorized compute kernels, and batch coercion across critical performance paths.

Expected impact: 2–10x speedup on partitioned SQL loads, 5–50x on string filter operations, and 3–5x on schema coercion pipelines.

docs.title: Where PyArrow Is Used Today
docs.text: Module Usage Limitation parquet/resource.py pyarrow.dataset for file discovery & partitioning Only extracts file paths; data read goes to Dask/pandas core/filesystem.py pyarrow.fs for Local/S3 filesystem bridges Used as a passthrough, not for compute data/schema.py PyArrow dtype string aliases ("int64[pyarrow]") Normalization only; no actual Arrow types core/connection_catalog.py Type hints for pyarrow.fs.FileSystem Type annotation only

docs.title: The Core Problem
docs.text:
Parquet Path:  Parquet → PyArrow (internal to Dask) → pandas partitions → Dask graph
SQL Path:      SQLAlchemy cursor → pd.DataFrame(rows) → apply_schema_map() → Dask

Data never materializes as a PyArrow Table in application code. Every operation — filtering, coercion, sorting, aggregation — goes through pandas, which means: - Row-by-row pandas construction from SQLAlchemy cursors (slow for large partitions) - Per-column coercion loops via pd.to_datetime(), pd.to_numeric(), .astype() - String operations via pandas .str.* methods (not vectorized) - No zero-copy concatenation for chunked IN-list results

docs.title: Phase 1: Arrow-Backed SQL Partition Loading (Highest Impact)
docs.text:
Target: data/db/partitioned_execution.py, data/db/sql_model_builder.py

Current hot path (runs for every SQL partition): 

# partitioned_execution.py:86-101
frame = pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=columns)
return SqlPartitionExecutor.align_and_coerce_partition(frame, meta_dtypes)

Proposed change: 

import pyarrow as pa

# Build Arrow Arrays directly from column buffers (zero-copy from driver where supported)
arrays = [pa.array([row[i] for row in rows], type=arrow_type) for i, arrow_type in enumerate(arrow_types)]
batch = pa.RecordBatch.from_arrays(arrays, names=columns)
table = pa.Table.from_batches([batch])

# Single-pass coercion instead of per-column loop
table = table.cast(target_arrow_schema)
return table.to_pandas(types_mapper=_get_dtype_mapper)  # or return Arrow directly

Benefits: - Eliminates per-row pandas DataFrame construction overhead - Replaces apply_schema_map() column-by-column loop with table.cast_to_schema() (single pass) - Estimated 2–5x speedup on large partition fetches

Implementation details: 1. Add data/db/arrow_schema_mapper.py — maps SQLAlchemy types to PyArrow types 2. Modify SqlPartitionExecutor.fetch_partition() to build Arrow batches 3. Add configuration flag use_arrow=True on DataGateway for opt-in migration 4. Maintain backward compatibility — fallback to pandas path when use_arrow=False

docs.title: Phase 2: Arrow Compute Kernels for Filter Operations
docs.text:
Target: data/filters/utils.py, data/filters/handler.py

Current limitations: - String operations (contains, startswith, regex) use pandas .str.* via map_partitions - $or/$not boolean operators excluded from pushdown — applied as residual pandas filters - Date casting in filters uses pd.Timestamp arithmetic

Proposed changes:

docs.title: 2a. Residual String Filters via PyArrow Compute
docs.text:
import pyarrow.compute as pc

# Current (slow):
column.map_partitions(lambda s: s.str.contains(pattern, na=False))

# Proposed (fast):
pc.match_substring(column_chunk, pattern=pattern)  # vectorized, zero-copy on Arrow chunk
pc.match_like(column_chunk, pattern)                # for LIKE patterns
pc.match_substring_regex(column_chunk, pattern)     # for regex

Implementation: 1. Add data/filters/arrow_kernels.py — PyArrow compute equivalents for all filter operations 2. Modify build_mask_fn() in handler.py to detect Arrow-backed columns and use pc.* kernels 3. Extend split_pushdown_and_residual() to include more operators in pushdown when Arrow is available

docs.title: 2b. $or/$not Boolean Operator Pushdown
docs.text:
# Current: $or returns empty pushdown, all applied as residual
# Proposed: Use PyArrow dataset expressions
import pyarrow.dataset as ds

ds.or_(filter_expr_a, filter_expr_b)
ds.invert(filter_expr)  # for $not

Benefits: - 5–50x speedup on string-heavy residual filters - Dramatically reduced memory usage (no intermediate pandas partitions for filtered data) - Better parquet pushdown coverage

docs.title: Phase 3: Arrow Schema as Canonical Contract
docs.text:
Target: data/schema.py, data/field_map.py

Current approach: 

# schema.py: dict-based dtype mapping + per-column coercion
SCHEMA_MAP = {"col_a": "Int64", "col_b": "boolean", "col_c": "datetime64[ns, UTC]"}
for col, dtype in schema_map.items():
    df[col] = _coerce_series(df[col], dtype)  # N separate passes

Proposed approach: 

# Define canonical PyArrow schema
ARROW_SCHEMA = pa.schema([
    ("col_a", pa.int64()),
    ("col_b", pa.bool_()),
    ("col_c", pa.timestamp("ns", tz="UTC")),
])

# Single-pass coercion
table = pa.Table.from_pandas(df)
table = table.cast(ARROW_SCHEMA)  # one operation, minimal copy

Implementation: 1. Add data/schema/arrow_schema.py — ArrowSchema class wrapping pa.Schema with: - from_dict() constructor from existing dict format - cast_table() method for single-pass coercion - equals() for validation (replaces validate_schema()) 2. Modify apply_schema_map() to use table.cast_to_schema() when Arrow is available 3. Add FieldMap.rename_table() — table.rename_columns() is O(1) (no data movement vs pandas rename)

Benefits: - 3–5x speedup on schema coercion (single pass vs N column loops) - Stronger schema contracts — pa.Schema has built-in equality, nullability, and metadata support - Cleaner dtype normalization — no more string alias parsing

docs.title: Phase 4: Arrow-Native DataGateway Path
docs.text:
Target: data/gateway/core.py, data/gateway/loaders.py

Current: DataGateway always returns pandas or Dask DataFrames.

Proposed: Add return_type parameter: "pandas" | "arrow" | "dask"

# New signature
gateway.load(
    query="...",
    return_type="arrow",  # new option
    filters={...},
)
# Returns: pa.Table (single partition) or list[pa.Table] (partitioned)

Data flow with Arrow path: 

SQL:     SQLAlchemy cursor → Arrow RecordBatch → pa.Table → (optional: to_pandas)
Parquet: pyarrow.dataset → pa.Table → (optional: to_dask / to_pandas)

Implementation: 1. Add return_type parameter to DataGateway.load(), load_all(), load_period(), semi_join(), etc. 2. Modify loaders (data/gateway/loaders.py) to produce Arrow Tables when requested 3. Add data/gateway/arrow_adapters.py — Arrow equivalents of Dask post-load transforms: - sort_by() via table.sort_by() - drop_duplicates() via table.group_by().aggregate() - concat_tables() via pa.concat_tables() (zero-copy) 4. Extend _apply_df_options() to _apply_table_options() for Arrow path

Benefits: - Users who don't need pandas can skip the conversion entirely - Downstream Arrow consumers (e.g., DuckDB, Polars, ML pipelines) get native input - Enables zero-copy interop with other Arrow-compatible libraries

docs.title: 5a. Parquet Statistics-Aware Partition Planning
docs.text:
Target: data/parquet/resource.py

Current file discovery only extracts paths. PyArrow datasets expose: - dataset.scanner().scan_statistics() — row counts, null counts, min/max per column - Fragment-level metadata — file sizes, row group info

Use cases: - Skip empty or irrelevant files before loading - Better partition sizing based on actual row counts - Predicate pushdown effectiveness estimation

docs.title: 5b. Arrow Memory-Mapped Reads for Large Parquet Files
docs.text:
import pyarrow.parquet as pq

# Current: full read into memory
table = pq.read_table(path)

# Proposed: memory-map for out-of-core processing
pf = pq.ParquetFile(path, memory_map=True)
table = pf.read_row_group(0)  # only needed row groups

docs.title: 5c. Dictionary Encoding for Categorical Columns
docs.text:
# Automatically dictionary-encode low-cardinality columns
table = table.combine_chunks()
table = table.replace_schema_metadata({"pandas_type": "categorical"})

Reduces memory footprint 5–20x for columns like status, country, type.

docs.title: 5d. IPC Serialization for Caching
docs.text:
# Arrow IPC format for fast intermediate caching
sink = pa.OSFile(path, "wb")
with pa.ipc.new_file(sink, table.schema) as writer:
    writer.write(table)

# Zero-copy read
with pa.ipc.open_file(path) as reader:
    table = reader.get_all()

Faster than parquet for write-once-read-many cached results.

docs.title: Implementation Roadmap
docs.text:
Phase Scope Estimated Effort Risk 1. Arrow SQL Loading partitioned_execution.py, new arrow_schema_mapper.py Medium Low — opt-in, backward compatible 2. Arrow Filter Kernels filters/utils.py, filters/handler.py, new arrow_kernels.py Medium Low — additive, no breaking changes 3. Arrow Schema Contract schema.py, field_map.py, new arrow_schema.py Low Low — wraps existing dict format 4. Arrow DataGateway Path gateway/core.py, loaders.py, new arrow_adapters.py High Medium — new API surface 5. Advanced Optimizations Statistics, memory-mapping, dictionary encoding, IPC Low each Low — optional features

Recommended order: Phase 1 → Phase 3 → Phase 2 → Phase 4 → Phase 5

Phase 1 gives the highest immediate ROI. Phase 3 strengthens the schema contract with minimal effort. Phase 2 builds on Phase 3's Arrow types. Phase 4 is the largest change but unlocks the full Arrow ecosystem.

docs.title: Risks and Mitigations
docs.text: Risk Mitigation PyArrow version compatibility Pin minimum version (pyarrow>=14.0.0), test against multiple versions Memory overhead Arrow is columnar — large wide tables may use more memory; use chunked arrays and combine_chunks() judiciously Type mapping gaps Start with common types (int, float, string, bool, timestamp); add edge cases incrementally Breaking changes All Arrow features opt-in via use_arrow=False default; no existing behavior changes Dependency bloat PyArrow is already a dependency; no new external deps for Phases 1–3

docs.title: Dependencies
docs.text:
Already present (in pyproject.toml): - pyarrow — core library - dask[dataframe] — uses PyArrow internally for parquet - fsspec — filesystem abstraction

No new dependencies required for Phases 1–4.

docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text:
Boti's architecture is well-positioned for PyArrow integration. The ManagedResource lifecycle, DataGateway abstraction, and existing PyArrow filesystem usage provide a clean foundation. By introducing Arrow as a first-class in-memory representation — starting with SQL partition loading and schema coercion — Boti can achieve significant performance gains without breaking changes or new dependencies.

The phased approach ensures: 1. Immediate value (Phase 1: 2–5x SQL load speedup) 2. Low risk (opt-in, backward compatible) 3. Progressive enhancement (each phase builds on the last) 4. No new dependencies (uses existing pyarrow)

Next step: Implement Phase 1 with a feature flag, benchmark against production workloads, and validate performance gains before proceeding.

docs.title: Security Hardening Guide
docs.text: This guide documents defensive defaults and validation hooks for SQL and Datacube paths in boti-data.

docs.title: Scope
docs.text:
• SQL reads through DataGateway and DataHelper
  • Datacube request validation via DatacubeContract
  • Distributed SQL worker credential handling

docs.title: Filter Interpolation Hotspots
docs.text:
Use this matrix during reviews to identify where dynamic filter/query inputs are accepted and what control should be enforced.

Module Entry point Risk type Recommended control src/boti_data/gateway/normalization.py split_control_and_filters(), normalize_configured_filters() Runtime kwargs not in LOAD_CONTROL_KEYS are treated as filters and merged with sticky/explicit filters. Restrict caller-provided kwargs shape and validate allowed filter keys at API boundary. src/boti_data/gateway/core.py _build_configured_request() Merged semantic filters are forwarded into SQL query construction. Enforce semantic field allowlists and keep field_map translation enabled where DB names differ. src/boti_data/field_map.py translate_filters_to_db() Dynamic filter keys are rewritten into DB-column keys, including nested boolean operators. Validate semantic keys before translation; reject unknown/suspicious operator forms. src/boti_data/filters/handler.py compile_filters(), apply_filters() Dynamic field__op expressions compile into backend-specific conditions. Keep operator parsing strict and test forbidden keys/ops in security regressions. src/boti_data/gateway/loaders.py _prepare_sql_statement() Raw sql text is accepted when allowed; app-side string interpolation can bypass intent. Prefer raw_sql_policy="disabled" for production and require bound params for any approved raw SQL. src/boti_data/parquet/reader.py _normalize_filter_options() Bare kwargs are promoted into filters, which may broaden query scope unexpectedly. Use explicit filters= in higher-risk call paths and lint/review wildcard runtime kwargs. src/boti_data/datacube/resource.py _prepare_request() Datacube filters/cube names are accepted unless contract validator is configured. Make DatacubeContract.request_validator mandatory in production configs.

docs.title: Raw SQL Is Denied by Default
docs.text: sql= execution requires an explicit allow_raw_sql=True opt-in. Without that flag, loads fail fast.

docs.title: Raw SQL Is Read-Only Only
docs.text: Even when enabled, only single-statement read-only SELECT/WITH queries are accepted. Mutating or multi-statement payloads are rejected.

docs.title: Disable Raw SQL Entirely
docs.text: For stricter deployments, initialize DataGateway(..., raw_sql_policy="disabled"). This blocks all sql= calls, including those with allow_raw_sql=True.

docs.title: Always Bind Parameters
docs.text:
Use bound parameters instead of string interpolation:

frame = gateway.load(
    sql="SELECT id, status FROM users WHERE status = :status",
    params={"status": status_value},
    as_pandas=True,
    allow_raw_sql=True,
)

Do not build SQL with f-strings or concatenated user input.

docs.title: Datacube Hardening
docs.text:
Datacube security policy is contract-driven. If no request_validator is configured, suspicious cubes/filter keys can be accepted by permissive loaders.

Use a strict validator to enforce business and security constraints:

def request_validator(request):
    cube_name = str(request.cube or "")
    if ".." in cube_name or "/" in cube_name:
        raise ValueError("cube name contains forbidden path tokens")
    if any(str(key).startswith("$") for key in request.filters):
        raise ValueError("operator-style filter keys are not allowed")

Attach it with DatacubeContract(request_validator=...).

You can enforce validator presence at gateway construction time:

gateway = DataGateway(
    DatacubeConfig(loader=loader, contract=contract),
    require_datacube_request_validator=True,
)

docs.title: Strict Filter Validation (Opt-In)
docs.text:
DataGateway supports optional strict controls for configured-mode and datacube filter payloads:

  • strict_filter_validation=True
  • allowed_filter_fields={...}
  • max_filter_depth=...
  • max_filter_conditions=...
  • max_in_filter_values=...

Example:

gateway = DataGateway(
    sql_config,
    table="users",
    strict_filter_validation=True,
    allowed_filter_fields={"status", "created_at"},
    max_filter_depth=6,
    max_filter_conditions=64,
    max_in_filter_values=1000,
)

docs.title: Distributed SQL Credential Handling
docs.text:
For distributed execution, set worker_connection_env_var on SqlDatabaseConfig so task payloads do not serialize raw DSNs:

config = SqlDatabaseConfig(
    connection_url="postgresql+psycopg://...",
    worker_connection_env_var="DB_DSN",
)

Ensure the configured env var is present on every worker.

uv run pytest -m security_regression

docs.title: Changelog
docs.text: All notable changes to boti-data are recorded here. The format follows Keep a Changelog and the project follows Semantic Versioning.

docs.title: Versioning policy
docs.text:
• Every name exported from boti_data is listed in exactly one of boti_data.STABLE and boti_data.EXPERIMENTAL.
  • Stable names keep their signature and behaviour across minor releases. A stable name is removed or changed incompatibly only in a major release, and is first deprecated for at least one minor release: accessing it emits a DeprecationWarning naming the removal version and the replacement.
  • Experimental names may change in any minor release. They are marked as such in the reference documentation and in this file when they change.
  • Patch releases contain fixes only. Minor releases add features and deprecations. Major releases (2.0 onwards) remove what was deprecated and may change stable behaviour, with a migration guide.
  • Floors on boti and boti-dask are raised in minor releases and recorded under "Changed", together with the compatibility matrix in the README.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• ADBC partition fetches behind the read-only guards (boti-data[adbc]): with the driver installed and query_only=True, PostgreSQL and SQLite partitions are fetched through ADBC, which returns Arrow straight from the wire protocol. The ADBC session gets the same read-only statement the SQLAlchemy engine issues, only the planner's compiled partitions are sent (psycopg placeholders are rewritten to $n), one connection is opened per fetch and closed with it (the workers' NullPool rule, so the fetch gate bounds open connections), and a driver error falls back to SQLAlchemy for that partition. adbc=False opts out.
  • Arrow-native partition fetch (boti_data.db.arrow_fetch): cursor results become pyarrow.Table in one columnar pass, using the driver's own Arrow reader where there is one (DuckDB) and raw DBAPI rows elsewhere, with a vectorised pyarrow.compute cast before any per-value coercion. A 1M-row SQLite partition fetch went from 2.93 s to 0.87 s; the Arrow and pandas paths produce identical frames.
  • Streaming results: DataGateway.iter_batches(...), SqlRepository.iter_batches() and AsyncSqlRepository.iter_batches() yield Arrow record batches through a server-side cursor, holding about one batch of memory however large the result.
  • Engine extras pandas, polars and dask; dataframes is now their union. No module imports dask, polars or boti-dask at import time (boti_data._engines loads them on first use), so a pandas-only install never loads Dask, and a missing engine is reported as the extra to add.
  • polars-native path: return_type="polars" is built from Arrow with no pandas detour for SQL and Parquet loads; ParquetDataResource.scan_polars() returns a lazy polars frame over the resource's filesystem.
  • Metrics and tracing (R8): boti_data.telemetry with a no-op default, an in-memory provider for tests and an OpenTelemetry provider behind the new otel extra, selected with telemetry.configure() or BOTI_DATA_TELEMETRY=otel. Spans around every gateway load and partition fetch, a histogram of fetch-gate waits, and pool checkout counter and checked-out gauge from SQLAlchemy pool events on every engine, keyed on the connection-URL digest, never the DSN. See the "Metrics and tracing" guide.
  • Cluster-wide partition fetch gate: on a Dask cluster the gate is boti_dask.cluster_semaphore, a scheduler-side semaphore shared by every worker, so max_concurrent_fetches bounds the whole cluster rather than each worker process. The gate is keyed on a hash of the database identity alone, never on the limit, so two loads with different limits share one gate (first limit wins, warning logged). Without a running client, or with boti-dask below 1.1.0, the process-wide gate applies as before.
  • Compatibility-matrix workflow testing the floor, locked and latest releases of boti and boti-dask on every push, weekly, and on an upstream-release repository dispatch; matrix published in the README.
  • s3 extra (boti-data[s3]) delegating to boti[s3] for s3fs, which boti 1.1.0 and later no longer install by default.
  • Public API contract: boti_data.STABLE and boti_data.EXPERIMENTAL stability tuples covering every exported name, boti_data.DEPRECATED with the boti_data._contract.deprecated helper wired into the lazy module __getattr__, and this changelog.
  • Benchmark suite under benchmarks/ (eight pytest-benchmark cases runnable against SQLite and local Parquet), a committed baseline, make bench and make bench-compare, and a workflow that fails a release when a median regresses by more than 20 percent.
  • Reference documentation site built with mkdocs-material and mkdocstrings, versioned with mike on release tags; README cut to installation, three examples and links.
  • Incremental loads: DataGateway.load(since=...) / aload(since=...) filter by a stored watermark and advance it after a successful load; SqlWatermarkStore keeps the watermark in a boti_watermarks table next to the data. Partitioned SQL loads are resumable: SqlPartitionedLoader .load_request(request, checkpoint=PlanCheckpoint(store, key)) persists each finished partition, and resume=True on the request fetches only the partitions still pending (SqlPartitionPlan.to_json()/from_json(), FileCheckpointStore). UpsertSink merges a frame into a SQL table with INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (PostgreSQL, SQLite), INSERT OR REPLACE (DuckDB) or ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE (MySQL), registered as the "upsert" sink. Guide: docs/guides/incremental-loads.md.

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
Findings of the 2026-11 audit, each with a regression test under tests/security/:

  • Partition values taken from the data (partition_on columns) are validated before any sink writes: a value that is empty, ., .., or contains /, \ or NUL fails the write. Such a value previously became a directory name and could place files outside the project root.
  • A parquet_storage_path with a scheme other than file:// is refused when the resource's filesystem is local. The scheme was stripped and the rest read as a local path, bypassing the sandbox on the Dask load path.
  • overwrite=False now appends. Dask names output files part.N from zero on every write, so a second write into an existing dataset replaced the first's files. Appended files carry a unique token in their name.
  • The raw-SQL guard also rejects INTO, SET, set_config, RESET, LOAD, INSTALL, EXPORT, IMPORT, lo_import, lo_export, setval, nextval and backend-termination functions. The guard remains a heuristic; database-enforced read-only (query_only=True) is the control to rely on.
  • DuckDB under query_only=True connects with enable_external_access off, locked at connect time. read_only protects the database file only; table functions such as read_text() and read_csv() could still read local files and, through httpfs, the network. Reading external files from a query-only DuckDB connection now needs query_only=False.
  • Async worker engines (AsyncSqlPartitionedLoader) now receive the same read-only session statement as sync worker engines; they validated support but never applied it.

Medium findings of the same audit, tests under tests/security/test_regressions_audit_mediums.py:

  • CsvSink/JsonlSink with a remote storage_path and no injected fs build the filesystem through boti's FilesystemConfig, so its endpoint validation (private and reserved addresses) applies. The previous fsspec fallback accepted any URL, including a loopback HTTP server.
  • ParquetSink writes to the path the resource resolved against the project root. A relative parquet_storage_path was written (and with overwrite=True, removed) relative to the working directory instead.
  • Engine registry keys and worker engine identities include a digest of connect_args and execution_options. Two configs with one DSN but different TLS settings shared an engine, the second silently getting the first's connections.
  • The read-only connect listener is attached before a new engine is registered (EngineRegistry.get_or_create(..., configure=)); it was attached afterwards, leaving a window in which another holder could check out an unconfigured pooled connection.
  • Dask contains, not_contains and icontains filters match literally, as the SQL twin's escaped LIKE does; they treated the value as a regex. regex/iregex patterns pass validate_regex_pattern on both backends.
  • The Parquet append guard unifies every existing file's schema, not the first file's, so an append can no longer narrow a column a later partition introduced.
  • SqlPartitionSpec.key() hashes the JSON form of the parameters, so a checkpoint reloaded from disk (dates stored as ISO strings) maps to the same partition keys and resumes instead of refetching everything.

Low findings of the same audit:

  • Overwrites stage into a per-run .staging-<token> directory, so two overwriters of one target no longer delete each other's in-progress output. Leftover staging directories from crashed runs are reported, not removed. Overwriting a bucket root is refused, since its staging sibling would be another bucket.
  • The unified read schema of an evolved Parquet dataset is cached per file list, so every footer is read once per dataset, not once per load.
  • Checkpoints store date, datetime, time and Decimal parameters with their type and restore them as such; a resumed partition bound ISO strings where the plan had bound dates.
  • columns= is resolved through the mapper like filter fields are; a name such as __table__ widened the projection to every column.
  • in_chunk_size must be at least 1 and in_chunk_concurrency between 1 and 64; any integer was accepted and became the thread count.
  • SqlRepository.update() rejects keys that are not mapped columns and keys of primary-key columns; any attribute name was assigned.
  • The security guide documents what a pickled resource carries (remote filesystem credentials) and that checkpoint plans hold bound filter values.

docs.text:
• boti-dask floor raised to 1.3.0: the fetch gate relies on cluster_semaphore(strict=False), and the shared-session rebind and primitives fixes of that release.
  • boti floor raised to 1.2.0: ParquetDataResource resolves a relative parquet_storage_path against the project root, which boti anchors there only from 1.2.0 (1.0.x anchored to the working directory).

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text:
• Async Arrow and polars SQL loads (aload(return_type="arrow" | "polars")) raised a TypeError after the Arrow-fetch change: the async loader still called the old row-list finaliser. Both paths now share one finaliser, and the async path is tested.
  • Reading a Parquet dataset whose files disagree on a column's type in a way Arrow cannot promote (int64 in some files, strings in others) failed, since 1.3.x on the first non-parsing value and since the schema-evolution read on unification. Such columns are now read as string, eagerly and through Dask, with a warning naming them; every value is kept.

  • Boolean coercion on pandas 3.1: a column whose values all miss the literal map (floats such as 1.0) came back as a null-typed Arrow series and the numeric fallback could not assign into it. The fallback now works on an object array. Caught by the compatibility matrix's "latest" jobs.

  • DataGateway is pickleable again on boti 1.0.11 and later: the boti Logger now holds a threading.Event, so the gateway's post-processor drops its logger on pickle and DataGateway.__setstate__ re-attaches the restored resource's logger.

  • Parquet discovery tests no longer patch the removed boti.core.secure_io.is_secure_path.

Last release before this changelog was kept. Sinks honour an injected filesystem on remote paths and reject NUL bytes for every scheme; the dataframes extra is named in the error when its dependencies are missing.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
Install directly:

pip install boti-data

Or install through the core package extra:

pip install "boti[data]"

boti-data doesn't bundle a database driver by default — SQLAlchemy resolves the driver package from your connection URL's scheme (mysql+pymysql://, postgresql+asyncpg://, ...), so install the one matching your database:

pip install "boti-data[mysql]"      # asyncmy + pymysql
pip install "boti-data[postgres]"   # asyncpg + psycopg[binary]
pip install "boti-data[clickhouse]" # clickhouse-connect (sync only)
pip install "boti-data[duckdb]"     # duckdb-engine (sync only)

Parquet storage on s3:// (including MinIO through fs_type=s3) needs s3fs, which boti 1.1.0 and later no longer install by default:

pip install "boti-data[s3]"         # boti[s3] -> s3fs
pip install "boti-data[adbc]"         # ADBC drivers: Arrow straight from PostgreSQL/SQLite on read-only partition fetches

ClickHouse support is sync-only: there is no maintained async SQLAlchemy driver for ClickHouse, so AsyncSqlDatabaseResource rejects a ClickHouse connection URL — use SqlDatabaseResource instead. SqlUnitOfWork/AsyncSqlUnitOfWork also reject ClickHouse outright, since ClickHouse's transaction support is experimental, single-node, and MergeTree-only, with no real cross-table ACID guarantees to back a multi-table unit of work — use SqlRepository/AsyncSqlRepository directly, one table at a time, instead.

Verified against a real ClickHouse instance:

  • SqlRepository/AsyncSqlRepository are a get/insert/update/delete-by-primary-key API, but MergeTree's ORDER BY is a sort/index prefix, not a uniqueness constraint — many real ClickHouse tables have several rows per ORDER BY key. Because of that, get()/update()/delete() each refuse to run against a ClickHouse table unless called with assume_unique_key=True (e.g. repo.get(pk, assume_unique_key=True)). This flag is a per-call caller assertion, not something boti-data verifies or enforces: it does not check the data, and if the key genuinely isn't unique, get(key, assume_unique_key=True) will still return one arbitrary matching row and delete(key, assume_unique_key=True)/update(key, ..., assume_unique_key=True) will still affect every row sharing that key, not just one. Only pass it once you've confirmed the key is actually unique for that table. insert() has no such parameter — appending a row is never ambiguous.
  • .update() also fails outright on a table without enable_block_number_column enabled (ALTER TABLE ... MODIFY SETTING enable_block_number_column = 1, off by default) — ClickHouse raises Lightweight updates are not supported otherwise.
  • query_only=True is enforced server-side (ClickHouse's readonly setting, applied via set_client_setting on connect), not just by boti-data's own read-only session guard.

DuckDB support is also sync-only (no maintained async driver, same as ClickHouse — AsyncSqlDatabaseResource rejects a DuckDB connection URL), but is otherwise a better fit than ClickHouse for SqlRepository's by-primary-key model:

  • SqlUnitOfWork/AsyncSqlUnitOfWork are fully supported — DuckDB has real multi-table ACID transactions (unlike ClickHouse), verified with an actual mid-transaction constraint violation correctly rolling back writes across two tables.
  • No assume_unique_key-style flag is needed — DuckDB genuinely enforces PRIMARY KEY/UNIQUE constraints at the database level, and boti-data recovers the real key columns from DuckDB's catalog even though duckdb-engine's own reflection can't see them (a known upstream limitation — it warns "doesn't yet support reflection on indices"). Without that recovery step, every DuckDB table would look keyless and SqlRepository would silently bind to an arbitrary first column instead of the real key — this was caught and fixed during implementation, not just assumed away.
  • query_only=True is enforced via a connect-time flag, not a runtime statement: DuckDB's read-only mode (duckdb.connect(read_only=True)) can only be set when a connection is opened, so boti-data injects connect_args={"read_only": True} itself before the engine is even constructed, rather than configuring it afterward the way Postgres/MySQL/ClickHouse do.
  • DuckDB allows only one process to hold a database file open for read-write at a time — opening a file in its default mode claims an exclusive lock on connect, even for a connection that only ever reads. SqlPartitionedLoader (which spawns one engine per worker process) requires query_only=True for a file-backed DuckDB DSN for exactly this reason — otherwise the first worker to connect would block every other worker, regardless of whether any of them write. Concurrent read-only access from multiple processes works fine. In-memory (duckdb:///:memory:) DSNs are rejected for distributed loading the same way SQLite's are, since each worker process would get its own independent, empty database.

If a Postgres table has a pgvector vector column, install boti-data[pgvector] too — this registers pgvector's Vector type with SQLAlchemy's reflection so SqlAlchemyModelBuilder/SqlRepository/DataGateway map that column to a usable list[float] (with its dimension preserved) instead of an unreflectable NullType:

pip install "boti-data[pgvector]"

The base install is deliberately light: single-row transactional access (SqlRepository/AsyncSqlRepository, see the SQL loads guide) works out of the box, with no dask/pandas/polars pulled in. The dataframe-shaped side of the package (DataGateway/DataHelper, ParquetPipeline, HybridDataset, the sink pipelines, ...) needs at least one engine extra:

pip install "boti-data[pandas]"      # pandas results; Dask is never imported
pip install "boti-data[polars]"      # polars results built from Arrow; pandas comes along for shaping
pip install "boti-data[dask]"        # lazy and distributed loads: dask[dataframe,distributed] + boti-dask
pip install "boti-data[dataframes]"  # the union of the three

Pick the engine with return_type ("pandas", "polars", "dask", or "arrow" for a pyarrow.Table, which needs no extra at all). A multi-partition SQL load to pandas with no Dask installed fetches partitions on a bounded thread pool instead of a task graph; the same max_concurrent_fetches limit applies. Asking for an engine that is not installed raises a ModuleNotFoundError naming the extra to add.

docs.title: ADBC partition fetches
docs.text: With the adbc extra installed, read-only partition fetches (query_only=True, the default) on PostgreSQL and SQLite go through the backend's ADBC driver, which returns Arrow straight from the wire protocol instead of DBAPI rows. ADBC sits outside SQLAlchemy, so boti-data re-applies the same guards before using it: the DSN must already pass the read-only validation (a SQLite DSN with mode=ro), the ADBC session gets the same read-only statement the SQLAlchemy engine issues on connect, and only the planner's compiled partition statements are ever sent, never raw SQL text. Writable connections, MySQL and ClickHouse, raw SQL and the async loader stay on SQLAlchemy. Set adbc=False on the SQL config to opt out; a driver error on a partition logs a warning and falls back to SQLAlchemy for that partition.

Base datacube with mutable .df and subclass-overridable transform hooks.

This module provides :class:BaseDataCube, an inheritance-based extension point for building data containers that load data via :class:DataHelper and optionally apply sync/async transforms after loading.

For composition-based datacube patterns, see :class:DatacubeResource and :class:DatacubeContract.

docs.title: BaseDataCube
docs.text:
BaseDataCube(**kwargs: Any)

Bases: PicklableLifecycleCoreMixin, LifecycleCore

Base datacube with mutable .df and subclass-overridable transform hooks.

Subclasses may override:

  • fix_data(**kwargs) — synchronous, local transforms.
  • afix_data(**kwargs) — asynchronous transforms (I/O, awaits).

Semantics:

  • load() → delegates to the internal :class:DataHelper, then runs fix_data() if the subclass overrides it.
  • aload() → delegates to the internal :class:DataHelper, then runs afix_data() if overridden, else falls back to fix_data().

class MyCube(BaseDataCube):
    config = {"table": "orders", "return_type": "pandas"}

    def fix_data(self, **kwargs):
        self.df = self.df[self.df["status"] == "active"]

cube = MyCube(dsn="postgresql://...")
df = cube.load()  # loads + filters

docs.title: boti_data.db.sql_repository
docs.text:
Lightweight single-row transactional access (get/insert/update/delete by primary key), returning plain dicts instead of a DataFrame — plus SqlUnitOfWork/AsyncSqlUnitOfWork for composing writes across several tables into one atomic transaction.

boti_data's flagship API (DataGateway/DataHelper) is dataframe-shaped and bulk-oriented, pulling in the dask/pandas/polars dependency chain even for a consumer that only ever touches one row at a time (e.g. an OLTP request handler at p95 <300ms). SqlRepository/AsyncSqlRepository sit directly on SqlDatabaseResource/AsyncSqlDatabaseResource + SqlModelRegistry — both already free of that dependency chain — so this module can be imported and used without dask/pandas/polars installed at all.

docs.title: SqlRepository
docs.text:
SqlRepository(
    config: SqlDatabaseConfig | None = None,
    table_name: str | None = None,
    *,
    schema: str | None = None,
    query_only: bool = True,
    session: Session | None = None,
)

Bases: LifecycleCore

Single-row get/insert/update/delete against one table, by primary key.

A thin repository layer over SqlDatabaseResource + SqlModelRegistry for consumers that want cheap transactional CRUD without pulling in DataGateway/DataHelper's dataframe-oriented machinery. Rows are plain dict[str, Any], never a DataFrame.

Exactly one of config/session must be given:

  • config: the repository owns a private SqlDatabaseResource and a fresh, query_only-guarded session per call, committing after every write. query_only defaults to True here and always wins over whatever config.query_only says — insert/update/delete raise via the same ReadOnlySession guard SqlDatabaseResource uses until a caller passes query_only=False explicitly. This is deliberate: a config object may be shared with or reused from a context where writes are already enabled, and a repository shouldn't silently inherit write access nobody asked it for.
  • session: an already-open Session supplied by the caller (e.g. from SqlUnitOfWork, or hand-rolled session code composing several repositories into one transaction). Writes flush() instead of commit() — the caller controls the transaction boundary — and closing this repository never closes the shared session. query_only is accepted for signature uniformity but is inert here: the session's own class (ReadOnlySession or not) already determines writability, since this path never constructs a new guarded session.

pk accepts a scalar or a tuple for composite keys, mirroring Session.get()'s own signature.

get()/update()/delete() each accept assume_unique_key, which must be explicitly passed as True to run against a ClickHouse table: ClickHouse's ORDER BY/primary key is a sort prefix, not a uniqueness constraint, so without this assertion those calls could silently touch the wrong row (get()) or every row sharing a key (update()/delete()) instead of just one. insert() is unaffected — appending a row is never ambiguous.

    config: SqlDatabaseConfig, *, query_only: bool = True
)

Shares one transaction across several SqlRepository instances, potentially against different tables, so their writes commit or roll back together.

Not a LifecycleCore subclass: LifecycleCore.__exit__ is marked @final specifically so cleanup-suppression logic can't be overridden, but that also means there's no hook that receives exception info to decide "commit on success, roll back on exception" — exactly what a unit of work needs. A small hand-rolled context manager is simpler than fighting that sealed contract.

docs.title: AsyncSqlDatabaseResource
docs.text:
AsyncSqlDatabaseResource(config: SqlDatabaseConfig)

Bases: LifecycleCore

Asynchronous context manager providing reflection/query-only SQLAlchemy access.

Async-only by design: real resource acquisition (the engine, session factory) happens in __aenter__, not __init__, since it requires awaiting EngineRegistry.get_or_create_async(). There is deliberately no sync close() support — see _cleanup() — because releasing a bound engine requires await EngineRegistry.release_async(); no sync path can do that safely. No pickle support either: even with LifecycleCore's own locks stripped, the SQLAlchemy AsyncEngine/ async_sessionmaker attributes below aren't picklable, and unlike the sync resources in this module there's no "reopen by DSN" pattern that would make reconstructing one on the other end meaningful.

DuckDB and ClickHouse have synchronous SQLAlchemy dialects only. For those DSNs engine and session are the executor-backed facades from :mod:boti_data.db.threaded_async (same connect()/begin()/ run_sync/session shape, blocking calls run in worker threads; no stream()), sharing the sync engine with SqlDatabaseResource via the registry. Bases: LifecycleCore

Asynchronous context manager providing reflection/query-only SQLAlchemy access.

Async-only by design: real resource acquisition (the engine, session factory) happens in __aenter__, not __init__, since it requires awaiting EngineRegistry.get_or_create_async(). There is deliberately no sync close() support — see _cleanup() — because releasing a bound engine requires await EngineRegistry.release_async(); no sync path can do that safely. No pickle support either: even with LifecycleCore's own locks stripped, the SQLAlchemy AsyncEngine/ async_sessionmaker attributes below aren't picklable, and unlike the sync resources in this module there's no "reopen by DSN" pattern that would make reconstructing one on the other end meaningful.

DuckDB and ClickHouse have synchronous SQLAlchemy dialects only. For those DSNs engine and session are the executor-backed facades from :mod:boti_data.db.threaded_async (same connect()/begin()/ run_sync/session shape, blocking calls run in worker threads; no stream()), sharing the sync engine with SqlDatabaseResource via the registry. A read-write DuckDB resource serialises its statements behind one asyncio.Lock; query_only=True reads run concurrently.

docs.title: boti_data.db.partitioned_fetch_gate
docs.text:
Partition-fetch concurrency gate and its contention accounting.

Split out of partitioned_execution.py purely for long-file headroom. Every name here is re-exported from partitioned_execution.py so existing import paths keep working unchanged.

The gate bounds how many partition fetches run at once, and the counters record how long fetches spent queueing for a slot. That second half exists because the gate is otherwise invisible: the diagnostics=True stage timers (db_fetch, prepare_stmt, load_plan) are all measured inside the gate, so under saturation total elapsed time rises while every stage timer still looks healthy. An idle database plus timing-out callers is the classic symptom, and without these counters it is indistinguishable from a database that is simply slow.

docs.text:
GateWaitStats(
    fetches: int = 0,
    waited_fetches: int = 0,
    total_wait_seconds: float = 0.0,
    max_wait_seconds: float = 0.0,
)

Time spent waiting for a partition-fetch slot, accumulated per process.

max_wait_seconds is cumulative for the life of the process and cannot be differenced into a per-load figure the way the other three can (a running maximum carries no record of when it was set). :meth:since therefore carries it through unchanged; it reads as "worst wait seen in this process so far", not "worst wait during this load".

docs.title: fetch_gate_stats
docs.text:
fetch_gate_stats() -> dict[str, GateWaitStats]

Snapshot partition-fetch gate contention for this process, by gate key.

Scope matters for interpreting the numbers. The gate itself is cluster-wide on a Dask cluster, but the wait counters are not: partition fetches are dispatched as Dask tasks, so in a distributed run each worker process accumulates its own counters and this function only ever sees the calling process's share. A lazy load returns before any fetch has run at all, so call this after .compute(), not after the load call returns.

Returning empty is deliberate rather than reporting zeros. docs.text:
DataGateway(
    config: BackendConfig,
    *,
    field_map: dict[str, str] | None = None,
    table: str | None = None,
    sticky_filters: dict[str, Any] | None = None,
    exclude: bool = False,
    df_params: DataFrameParams | None = None,
    df_options: DataFrameOptions | None = None,
    fs: AbstractFileSystem | None = None,
    fs_factory: Any | None = None,
    raw_sql_policy: str | None = None,
    policies: GatewayPolicies | None = None,
    strict_filter_validation: bool = False,
    allowed_filter_fields: set[str] | None = None,
    require_datacube_request_validator: bool = False,
)

Bases: PicklableLifecycleCoreMixin, LifecycleCore

Dask-first gateway that delegates to existing backend resources.

There are two usage modes:

Structured mode (default) Pass explicit statement, model, filters, etc. to :meth:load / :meth:aload exactly as before.

Configured mode Set table= at construction time. All keyword arguments passed to :meth:load / :meth:aload that are not control keywords are treated as runtime filter values and merged with sticky_filters.

All filter keys and ``fieldnames`` are always expressed as **semantic
names** (the right-hand side of *field_map*).  When a ``field_map`` is
provided the gateway translates them to DB column names before the query
and renames results back to semantic names on return.  When no
``field_map`` is given the DB is assumed to already use semantic names
and no translation is performed.

Pass ``exclude=True`` to invert the combined filter — the query returns
all rows that do **not** match the specified conditions (``WHERE NOT
(condition1 AND condition2 AND ...)``).

Example::

    gw = DataGateway(
        SqlDatabaseConfig(connection_url=SecretStr(db_url)),
        table="asm_tracking_productos",
        field_map=product_fields,      # present → DB has legacy names
        sticky_filters={"product_type_id": 1},
        exclude=True,                  # return rows where type != 1
    )
    df = await gw.aload(global_track_id=1)   # returns Dask DataFrame
    df = df.compute()
