from boti_data import DatacubeConfig, DatacubeContract, DataGateway


def loader(request):
    frame = pd.DataFrame({"id": [1, 2], "status": ["active", "inactive"]})
    if request.filters.get("status__exact") == "active":
        frame = frame[frame["status"] == "active"]
    return frame


contract = DatacubeContract(
    request_transformer=lambda request: request.model_copy(update={"cube": request.cube or "orders_v2"}),
    frame_transformer=lambda frame, request: frame.assign(cube=request.cube),
)

with DataGateway(
    DatacubeConfig(loader=loader, default_cube="orders", contract=contract),
    table="orders",
    sticky_filters={"status__exact": "active"},
) as gateway:
    df = gateway.load(return_type="pandas")

You can also configure this path with DataGateway.from_config({"backend": "datacube", ...}) or DataHelper({"backend": "datacube", ...}).

See the datacube contract notes for hook ordering, loader precedence, and validator rejection guidance. See the security hardening notes for SQL/raw-sql policy and distributed credential hardening defaults. For a runnable rejection flow, see examples/data_facade_datacube_contract_rejection.py.

docs.title: Distributed usage with Dask
docs.text: For large datasets or cluster workloads, DataHelper integrates natively with Dask. The DataHelper.session() factory creates a DaskSession that manages cluster and client lifecycle.

docs.title: Local cluster (development)
docs.text:
from dask.distributed import LocalCluster
from boti_data import DataHelper, SqlDatabaseConfig

config = SqlDatabaseConfig(
    connection_url="mysql+pymysql://user:pass@host/mydb",
    query_only=True,
    worker_connection_env_var="DB_URL",  # see the distributed guide
)

with DataHelper.session(cluster_factory=LocalCluster) as client:
    with DataHelper(config, table="orders") as helper:
        # Returns dask.dataframe.DataFrame — lazy, partitioned
        ddf = helper.dask.load(status="confirmed")

        # Trigger computation
        df = ddf.compute()

docs.title: Remote cluster
docs.text:
with DataHelper.session(scheduler_address="tcp://scheduler:8786") as client:
    with DataHelper(config, table="events") as helper:
        ddf = helper.dask.load(region="EU", return_type="dask")
        result = ddf.groupby("customer_id").agg({"amount": "sum"}).compute()

docs.title: Persisting on the cluster
docs.text:
Use persist=True to push the loaded data into distributed memory before further computation. This avoids re-reading from the database on every downstream operation:

with DataHelper.session(scheduler_address="tcp://scheduler:8786") as client:
    with DataHelper(config, table="transactions") as helper:
        # Data is loaded and held in cluster memory
        ddf = helper.load(year=2024, persist=True)

        # Subsequent operations reuse the persisted graph
        monthly = ddf.groupby("month").agg({"amount": "sum"}).compute()
        by_region = ddf.groupby("region").size().compute()

        # Preview persisted data before the managed session closes.
        sample = helper.load(year=2024, limit=5, persist=True).compute()

docs.title: Shared sessions for repeated notebook cells
docs.text:
When repeated cells need to reuse the same scheduler connection, opt into shared-session reuse explicitly:

with DataHelper.session(
    scheduler_address="tcp://scheduler:8786",
    shared=True,
    shared_key="notebook-main-cluster",
) as client:
    with DataHelper(config, table="transactions") as helper:
        ddf = helper.dask.load(year=2024)

docs.title: HybridDataset distributed pattern
docs.text:
Use this pattern when you split reads across historical and live sources but want one distributed execution context. HybridDataset composes two helpers, and DataHelper.session(...) keeps scheduler ownership explicit.

import asyncio

from dask.distributed import LocalCluster
from boti_data import DataHelper, HybridDataset

historical = DataHelper(backend="sqlalchemy", connection_url="sqlite:///events.db", table="events_hist")
live = DataHelper(backend="sqlalchemy", connection_url="sqlite:///events.db", table="events_live")
dataset = HybridDataset(historical, live, date_field="event_date", split_date="2026-04-18")

with LocalCluster(n_workers=1, threads_per_worker=1, processes=False, dashboard_address=":0") as cluster:
    with DataHelper.session(
        scheduler_address=cluster.scheduler_address,
        verify_connectivity=True,
        shared=True,
        shared_key="hybrid-dataset-distributed",
    ):
        ddf = dataset.dask.load(start="2026-04-14", end="2026-04-19", diagnostics=True)
        frame = ddf.compute()
        eager_frame = asyncio.run(
            dataset.aload(start="2026-04-16", end="2026-04-18", return_type="pandas")
        )

For a complete runnable script, see examples/data_hybrid_dataset_distributed.py.

docs.title: Semi-join across distributed frames
docs.text:
import pandas as pd

active_customers = pd.Series([1001, 1002, 1003, 1099])

with DataHelper(config, table="orders") as helper:
    # Loads only rows where customer_id is in active_customers
    ddf = helper.semi_join(active_customers, on="customer_id")
    df = ddf.compute()

semi_join also accepts Dask Series, enabling fully lazy distributed joins:

with DataHelper(config, table="customers") as customer_helper:
    with DataHelper(config, table="orders") as order_helper:
        active_ids = customer_helper.dask.load(active=True)["customer_id"]

        # Lazy — no computation happens yet
        orders_ddf = order_helper.semi_join(active_ids, on="customer_id")

        # Single compute triggers both loads
        result = orders_ddf.compute()

docs.title: The pickleable setting in distributed systems
docs.text:
When Dask distributes tasks across workers, it serialises (pickles) the task function and all its arguments to send them over the network. This creates a problem: database connection objects, engine pools, and credentials cannot be pickled.

boti-data addresses this through the worker_connection_env_var setting on SqlDatabaseConfig.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
Instead of serialising the full SqlDatabaseConfig (which contains the connection URL and credentials), boti-data extracts a minimal WorkerSqlConfig for each worker task. If worker_connection_env_var is set, workers read the DSN from that environment variable instead of having it embedded in the task payload.

Scheduler                              Worker
─────────                              ──────
SqlDatabaseConfig (full config)        WorkerSqlConfig (minimal, safe to pickle)
  connection_url = "mysql://..."   →     connection_env_var = "DB_URL"
  pool_size = 10                         query_only = True
  ...                                    pool_recycle = 1800
                                         (reads DB_URL from os.environ on worker)

docs.title: Setting it up
docs.text:
Step 1. Set the environment variable on all workers. For a local cluster:

export DB_URL="mysql+pymysql://user:pass@host/mydb"

For a Kubernetes-deployed cluster, inject it as a secret.

Step 2. Reference the variable in your config:

from boti_data import DataHelper, SqlDatabaseConfig

config = SqlDatabaseConfig(
    connection_url="mysql+pymysql://user:pass@host/mydb",
    query_only=True,
    worker_connection_env_var="DB_URL",  # workers use this instead of pickling credentials
)

Step 3. Use DataHelper normally. Credential serialisation is handled transparently:

with DataHelper.session(scheduler_address="tcp://scheduler:8786") as client:
    with DataHelper(config, table="orders") as helper:
        ddf = helper.dask.load(status="confirmed")
        result = ddf.compute()

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text:
Without worker_connection_env_var, using a real database DSN with distributed Dask will either:

  • fail with a pickle error (connection pool objects are not serialisable)
  • embed plaintext credentials in task payloads that flow through scheduler memory and worker logs

Setting worker_connection_env_var prevents both problems and is the recommended approach for any distributed SQL workflow.

docs.title: Dask resilience helpers
docs.text:
boti-data integrates with boti_dask for opt-in Dask runtime and resilience workflows.

Available helpers:

  • inspect_graph(...)
  • safe_compute(...)
  • safe_head(...)
  • safe_gather(...)
  • safe_persist(...)
  • safe_wait(...)
  • async_safe_compute(...)
  • async_safe_head(...)
  • async_safe_gather(...)
  • async_safe_persist(...)
  • async_safe_wait(...)
  • dask_is_probably_empty(...)
  • dask_is_empty(...)
  • UniqueValuesExtractor
  • apply_recommended_dask_config(...)

docs.title: Core rules
docs.text:
• Dask DataFrame-like graphs do not silently fall back to local threaded compute.
  • Retry behaviour is limited to recoverable communication failures.
  • The helpers are opt-in and designed to complement explicit DaskSession ownership.

docs.title: Minimal example
docs.text:
import asyncio
import dask
import dask.dataframe as dd
import pandas as pd

from boti_dask import (
    apply_recommended_dask_config,
    async_safe_compute,
    dask_session,
    inspect_graph,
    safe_compute,
    safe_persist,
    safe_wait,
)

frame = dd.from_pandas(pd.DataFrame({"id": [1, 2, 3]}), npartitions=2)

with apply_recommended_dask_config():
    with dask_session(cluster_kwargs={"n_workers": 1, "threads_per_worker": 1, "processes": False}) as client:
        metrics = inspect_graph(frame)
        persisted = safe_persist(frame, dask_client=client)
        safe_wait(persisted, dask_client=client)
        total = safe_compute(frame["id"].sum(), dask_client=client)
        preview = safe_head(frame, n=2, dask_client=client)

        async def run_async() -> int:
            delayed_value = dask.delayed(lambda: 6 * 7)()
            return await async_safe_compute(delayed_value, dask_client=client)

        async_total = asyncio.run(run_async())

docs.title: Dry-run and preview on gateway loads
docs.text:
Use dry_run=True to build and inspect a lazy Dask load graph without materializing it, and limit= to safely sample rows inside the session:

with DataHelper.session(scheduler_address="tcp://scheduler:8786", verify_connectivity=True) as client:
    with DataHelper(config, table="transactions") as helper:
        ddf = helper.dask.load(year=2024, dry_run=True, diagnostics=True)
        sample = helper.dask.load(year=2024, limit=5).compute()

docs.title: Resilient joins
docs.text:
For large indexed distributed joins, opt into resilient persistence:

joined = helper.left_join(
    left,
    right,
    join_key="id",
    join_schema_map={"id": "Int64"},
    persist=True,
    resilient=True,
    diagnostics=True,
)

docs.title: Sizing connections and fetch concurrency
docs.text:
More database connections do not mean more throughput. Past a modest number they mean less, because connections compete for the same cores, disks and locks. Both the PostgreSQL wiki and the HikariCP pool-sizing guide give the same starting formula:

connections = (core_count * 2) + effective_spindle_count

Count physical cores, not hyperthreads, and take effective_spindle_count as zero when the working set is cached in RAM. For a 4-core server with one disk that is about 10 connections in total — not per client, not per worker, in total.

The characteristic failure of getting this wrong is counter-intuitive: the database sits nearly idle, at a few percent CPU, while clients time out. The connections are all queued rather than working. Raising the pool size makes it worse.

boti-data exposes three separate numbers that multiply into that total. Size the product, not the individual knobs.

docs.title: 1. Client-side pool: pool_size + max_overflow
docs.text:
SqlDatabaseConfig defaults to pool_size=5 and max_overflow=10, so a single engine bursts to 15 connections, not 5. max_overflow is three times pool_size, so the steady-state number is a third of the real ceiling.

config = SqlDatabaseConfig(
    connection_url="postgresql+psycopg://...",
    pool_size=5,       # steady state
    max_overflow=10,   # burst headroom — the ceiling is 5 + 10 = 15
)

Engines are cached per distinct configuration, so two differently-configured helpers against the same database hold two pools: 30 connections, not 15.

docs.title: 2. Distributed fetch concurrency: n_workers × max_concurrent_fetches
docs.text:
max_concurrent_fetches (default 4, capped at 16) bounds concurrent partition fetches across the whole cluster: the gate is a boti_dask.cluster_semaphore held on the Dask scheduler and shared by every worker, keyed on the database alone. Twenty workers at max_concurrent_fetches=4 open at most 4 fetch connections to that database, so the number means what it reads.

Two things keep it honest:

  • One limit per database. Two loads against the same database with different limits share one gate; the first limit seen wins and a warning is logged. Limits never add up.
  • No cluster, no scheduler gate. In a local threads run, or with boti-dask older than 1.1.0, the same gate bounds the process instead, so a run with several processes against one database multiplies: n_processes × max_concurrent_fetches.

With the 10-connection budget above, leave headroom for the client-side pool and set max_concurrent_fetches to the remainder, whatever the worker count.

docs.title: 3. Worker connections are unpooled by design
docs.text:
Worker engines always use NullPool. Connection pools cannot be pickled and would bind to the wrong event loop, so each partition fetch opens a fresh connection and closes it. That is correct for distribution, but it means every fetch pays a full TCP handshake, TLS negotiation and authentication — on a remote database, tens of milliseconds each, before a single row is read. A 200-partition load pays it 200 times.

The fix is not to pool inside the workers, but to put a pooler in front of the database, so that warm server-side connections are reused while workers keep opening cheap local ones. The pooling mode matters, because it interacts with query_only:

Pooler mode Connection reuse query_only=True Session (e.g. PgBouncer session) Yes Supported — the read-only SET lasts for the session Transaction (e.g. PgBouncer transaction) Higher Not supported — see below

query_only=True issues its read-only statement on the SQLAlchemy connect event, so it applies to a physical connection. Under transaction-mode pooling a physical connection can be handed to a different logical client between transactions, and that session state is not guaranteed to survive the handoff. The failure is silent: a load that believes it is read-only quietly stops being so.

With transaction-mode pooling, set query_only=False and enforce read-only access with database grants instead, where it cannot be lost in a handoff.

docs.title: Measuring it
docs.text:
Set diagnostics=True on a partitioned load and the completion line reports how long fetches spent queueing for a slot:

Partitioned SQL load completed strategy=offset partitions=4 rows=40 result_partitions=1
  elapsed=0.04s prepare_stmt=0.000s load_plan=0.031s
  gate_waits=0/4 gate_wait_total=0.000s gate_wait_max_seen=0.000s

gate_waits=0/4 means none of the four fetches had to wait. A rising gate_wait_total alongside a database that is not CPU-bound is the signature of the failure above — concurrency queued rather than working. The other stage timers cannot show this, because they are all measured inside the gate.

The fields are omitted entirely when no fetch ran in the logging process. A lazy load returns a Dask graph before anything is fetched, and in a distributed run the fetches happen in other processes; reporting 0.000s there would say "no contention" when the truth is "not measured here".

For lazy loads, read the counters after .compute() instead:

from boti_data import fetch_gate_stats, reset_fetch_gate_stats

reset_fetch_gate_stats()
result = helper.dask.load().compute()

for gate_key, stats in fetch_gate_stats().items():
    print(gate_key, stats.waited_fetches, "/", stats.fetches, stats.total_wait_seconds)

fetch_gate_stats() reports the calling process only. On a distributed cluster each worker accumulates its own counters, so run it on the workers (e.g. via client.run(fetch_gate_stats)) to see the whole picture.

docs.title: Choosing between distributed and non-distributed
docs.text:
Use the following as a guide:

Scenario Recommended approach Exploratory analysis in a notebook helper.pandas.load() — simple, no overhead Single-machine pipeline, large-ish data helper.polars.load() — fast, low memory Result size unknown at design time helper.load(return_type="auto") — adapts Data does not fit in one machine's RAM helper.dask.load() + local or remote cluster Heavy transforms over millions of rows helper.dask.load() + Dask cluster Async service (FastAPI, ASGI) await helper.pandas.aload() or await helper.dask.aload() Sync script that needs async load path helper.aload_sync(...) Joining two large tables on a cluster helper.semi_join(series, on="key") Scheduled overnight batch job Dask cluster + persist=True for multi-pass jobs

Rule of thumb: start with pandas, switch to polars when single-machine performance matters, and move to dask when data size exceeds available RAM or when the task benefits from parallelism across workers.

docs.title: Incremental loads
docs.text: Three pieces turn a full reload into an incremental one: a watermark that remembers how far the last load got, a checkpoint that lets a long partitioned load resume where it stopped, and an upsert sink that merges the new rows into a table instead of appending duplicates.

docs.title: Loading only what changed: load(since=...)
docs.text:
DataGateway.load and aload accept an opt-in since= keyword. Give it the name of the watermark column and a store, and the gateway loads only rows above the stored watermark, computes the result, and advances the watermark to the new maximum before returning the frame.

from boti_data import DataGateway
from boti_data.db import SqlDatabaseConfig
from boti_data.watermark import FileWatermarkStore

store = FileWatermarkStore(".watermarks.json")
config = SqlDatabaseConfig(connection_url="postgresql://.../warehouse")

with DataGateway(config, table="events") as gateway:
    frame = gateway.load(since="updated_at", watermark_store=store, as_pandas=True)

The watermark is keyed by a source name, which defaults to the configured table. In structured mode (no table=), or to share one key between several gateways, pass watermark_source= or the long form:

frame = gateway.load(since=("updated_at", store, "events-hourly"), as_pandas=True)

Two further keywords tune the comparison: watermark_operator= ("gt" by default, "ge" to include rows equal to the watermark) and watermark_initial= for the first run when nothing is stored yet. The watermark only advances when the load succeeds, so a failed run is simply re-run.

docs.title: Where the watermark lives
docs.text:
Store Use when FileWatermarkStore(path) One process, local disk. Atomic rename on write. FsspecWatermarkStore(fs, path) Shared object storage between workers. SqlWatermarkStore(engine) The watermark should live next to the data, in the same database, under the same backups and permissions.

SqlWatermarkStore keeps one row per source in a boti_watermarks table (source, value, updated_at), created on first use. Values are JSON-encoded exactly as the file stores encode them, so a watermark can be moved between stores without conversion.

import sqlalchemy as sa
from boti_data.watermark import SqlWatermarkStore

store = SqlWatermarkStore(sa.create_engine("postgresql://.../warehouse"))

docs.title: Resuming an interrupted partitioned load
docs.text:
A partitioned SQL load fetches its plan partition by partition. Give SqlPartitionedLoader.load_request a PlanCheckpoint and every partition's frame is written to the checkpoint store the moment it is materialised. If the process dies after partition 37 of 100, re-run with resume=True on the request: the stored plan is reused, the 37 finished partitions are read back from the store, only the remaining 63 are fetched, and the returned frame is complete.

from boti_data.db import (
    FileCheckpointStore,
    PlanCheckpoint,
    SqlPartitionedLoader,
    SqlPartitionedLoadRequest,
)

store = FileCheckpointStore("/var/lib/etl/checkpoints")
request = SqlPartitionedLoadRequest(
    statement=select(Event), model=Event, chunk_size=50_000, as_pandas=True, resume=True
)
with SqlPartitionedLoader(config) as loader:
    frame = loader.load_request(request, checkpoint=PlanCheckpoint(store, "events-2026-11"))

Without resume=True the checkpoint starts afresh: the stored plan and frames are discarded and a new plan is written. A partition is done when its Parquet file exists in the store; there is no separate status file to fall out of step, so copies of the checkpoint held by several Dask tasks never disagree.

SqlPartitionPlan.to_json() and from_json() serialise the plan itself, so a plan computed once can be inspected, stored or handed to another process.

FileCheckpointStore keeps one directory per checkpoint key under its root, holding plan.json and one <partition>.parquet per finished partition. Implement the CheckpointStore protocol (five methods) to keep checkpoints elsewhere.

docs.title: Merging rows with UpsertSink
docs.text:
UpsertSink writes a frame into a SQL table with insert-or-update semantics on the given key columns. The target table must exist with a primary key or unique constraint on those columns.

from boti_data.pipelines import UpsertSink

with UpsertSink({"connection_url": url}, table="items", key_columns=["id"]) as sink:
    sink.write(frame)
Database Statement PostgreSQL, SQLite INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (keys) DO UPDATE SET ... DuckDB INSERT OR REPLACE INTO ... MySQL INSERT ... ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE ...

The dialect is detected from the engine. pandas, Arrow and polars frames are written in one transaction in chunks of chunk_rows (5,000 by default); a Dask frame is written partition by partition. The sink implements the PipelineSink protocol, so it can be used through SinkPipeline and the sink registry under the name "upsert", with table and key_columns in the sink configuration.

Putting the three together gives a pipeline that loads only new rows, survives an interruption without refetching, and lands the result without duplicates:

frame = gateway.load(since="updated_at", watermark_store=watermarks, as_pandas=True)
sink.write(frame)

docs.title: Parquet
docs.text: Parquet datasets as sources, as the target of ParquetPipeline, and composed with a live SQL table through HybridDataset.

docs.title: Parquet sources
docs.text:
from boti_data import DataHelper, ParquetDataConfig

config = ParquetDataConfig(
    parquet_storage_path="/data/orders/",
    parquet_start_date=date(2024, 1, 1),
    parquet_end_date=date(2024, 3, 31),
)

with DataHelper(config) as helper:
    df = helper.pandas.load()
    df = helper.polars.load()

docs.title: Lazy polars scans
docs.text: ParquetDataResource.scan_polars(columns=...) returns a pl.LazyFrame over the dataset, read through the resource's own (sandboxed) filesystem. Nothing is read until .collect(), and polars pushes column and filter selection into the scan.

docs.title: Date-bounded Parquet source
docs.text:
from boti_data import DataHelper, ParquetDataConfig
from datetime import date

config = ParquetDataConfig(
    parquet_storage_path="/data/warehouse/orders/",
    parquet_start_date=date(2024, 1, 1),
    parquet_end_date=date(2024, 6, 30),
)

with DataHelper(config) as helper:
    df = helper.pandas.load()
    ddf = helper.dask.load()  # lazy, partitioned read

docs.title: ParquetPipeline
docs.text:
ParquetPipeline is the first orchestration layer built on top of DataHelper and HybridDataset. It materialises a lazy source load into a parquet dataset directory and can optionally reload the written dataset through ParquetReader.

from boti_data import DataHelper, ParquetPipeline

helper = DataHelper(
    backend="sqlalchemy",
    connection_url=f"sqlite:///{db_path}",
    poolclass="sqlalchemy.pool.NullPool",
    query_only=False,
    table="source_events",
)

pipeline = ParquetPipeline(
    helper,
    {
        "backend": "parquet",
        "storage_path": "/tmp/source_events_dataset",
        "partition_on": ["partition_date"],
    },
    date_field="event_date",
)

result = pipeline.materialize(
    filters={"status__exact": "active"},
    reload=True,
    reload_options={"filters": {"partition_date__exact": "2026-04-17"}},
)

assert result.reloaded is True
frame = result.frame

Use materialize() / amaterialize() for the one-step workflow, or call to_parquet() and from_parquet() separately when you want explicit control over the write and reload phases. See examples/data_parquet_pipeline.py for a runnable end-to-end example.

docs.title: HybridDataset — historical + live composition
docs.text:
historical = DataHelper(backend="parquet", storage_path="/data/historical", parquet_filename="orders")
live = DataHelper(backend="sqlalchemy", connection_url="sqlite:///live.db", table="orders_live")

dataset = HybridDataset(
    historical,
    live,
    date_field="order_date",
    split_date="2026-04-18",
)

# mixed window (auto -> dask for hybrid composition)
ddf = dataset.load(start="2026-04-15", end="2026-04-20", return_type="auto")

# explicit source override through engine-bound view
pdf = dataset.pandas.load(start="2026-04-18", end="2026-04-20", source="live")

docs.title: Connection catalog
docs.text:
from boti_data import ConnectionCatalog, DataHelper

catalog = ConnectionCatalog()
catalog.load_sql("prod", prefix="PROD_DB_")  # reads PROD_DB_URL, PROD_DB_POOL_SIZE, etc.
catalog.load_sql("reporting", prefix="REPORT_DB_")

prod_config = catalog.sql_config("prod")
report_config = catalog.sql_config("reporting")

with DataHelper(prod_config, table="orders") as helper:
    df = helper.pandas.load(status="confirmed")

docs.title: Parquet in distributed settings
docs.text:
Parquet resources use fsspec for filesystem access. The filesystem object is not pickled directly; instead, ParquetDataResource uses a fs_factory callable or a filesystem_profile name that workers can use to reconstruct the filesystem independently. When filesystem_profile is used, filesystem creation is routed through ConnectionCatalog adapters so retry/cache behaviour stays consistent.

from boti_data import DataHelper, ParquetDataConfig, ConnectionCatalog

catalog = ConnectionCatalog()
catalog.load_filesystem("s3_prod", prefix="S3_")  # reads S3_ENDPOINT, S3_KEY, etc.

config = ParquetDataConfig(
    filesystem_profile="s3_prod",  # workers resolve filesystem from catalog
    parquet_storage_path="s3://my-bucket/orders/",
)

with DataHelper.session(cluster_factory=LocalCluster) as client:
    with DataHelper(config) as helper:
        ddf = helper.dask.load()
        result = ddf.compute()

docs.title: Security
docs.text: boti-data inherits its security posture from boti and adds SQL-specific guards on top. The regression suite under tests/security/ (30 tests, marked security_regression) pins every fix below; CI runs it on every push.

docs.title: Sandboxed paths and filesystems
docs.text: Every file-backed resource (ParquetDataResource, the sinks, the watermark stores) is a boti SecureResource: paths are resolved against the project root and refused when they escape it, NUL bytes are rejected for every scheme, and remote filesystems built from a ConnectionCatalog profile go through boti's SSRF-guarded fsspec adapters. Injected filesystems are honoured on remote paths rather than silently replaced.

docs.title: Read-only database access
docs.text: query_only=True (the default for SqlRepository/AsyncSqlRepository) makes the engine read-only at the connection level, enforced server-side where the backend supports it: PostgreSQL and MySQL set the session read-only on connect, ClickHouse applies its readonly setting, and DuckDB opens the file with read_only=True. It always overrides a passed-in config's own query_only, so a repository never inherits write access nobody asked for. Transaction-mode poolers can lose that session state between hand-offs; see Sizing connections.

docs.title: Raw SQL
docs.text: DataGateway accepts raw sql="..." only on eager paths, validated as a single read-only SELECT/WITH statement, and only when the call site opts in with allow_raw_sql=True under the default raw_sql_policy="readonly_opt_in". raw_sql_policy="disabled" blocks it outright. Lazy and partitioned loads always take statement + model, so every query a worker runs is compiled by SQLAlchemy with bound parameters. See the SQL loads guide.

docs.title: Credentials in distributed runs
docs.text: Workers never receive a SqlDatabaseConfig. They get a minimal WorkerSqlConfig, and when worker_connection_env_var is set they read the DSN from their own environment, so no credential crosses the scheduler or lands in a task payload or a worker log. The cluster-wide fetch gate is named by a hash of the engine identity for the same reason: the name reaches the scheduler and its dashboard. See the distributed guide.

docs.title: Pickling is opt-in twice
docs.text:
A resource pickles only when its config sets allow_pickle=True, and unpickles only in a process that has opted in with BOTI_ALLOW_TRUSTED_RESOURCE_UNPICKLE=1 or trusted_unpickle_scope(). The gate is an acknowledgement, not a sanitiser: pickle runs a payload's __reduce__ before any class-level hook can inspect it, so unpickling a payload from an untrusted source is still arbitrary code execution. Enable it only where every producer is trusted.

A pickled resource carries what it needs to work on a worker, and for a remote dataset that includes its FilesystemConfig with the access key and secret. Ship pickles only over transports you trust (TLS between Dask client, scheduler and workers), and prefer a worker_connection_env_var or a catalog profile name over embedded credentials where the resource supports it.

docs.title: Checkpoints and watermarks
docs.text: FileCheckpointStore and FileWatermarkStore take a plain root directory. Keys are validated to be simple names, never paths, so a key cannot leave the root; the root itself is yours to place. A plan checkpoint stores the compiled partition SQL and its bound parameter values, so filter values (which may be personal data) sit in plan.json under that root for as long as the checkpoint lives: clear checkpoints when a load completes.

docs.title: Logging
docs.text:
The boti logger redacts secrets, and diagnostics lines log counts, engine names and timings, never row data.

Further reading: security hardening notes.

docs.title: SinkPipeline and sinks
docs.text:
Phase 3 adds a minimal sink/plugin layer next to ParquetPipeline.

  • SinkPipeline orchestrates DataHelper / HybridDataset loads into any sink implementing the pipeline sink contract
  • CsvSink and JsonlSink are write-only dataset sinks (.csv / .jsonl shards)
  • ParquetPipeline now uses the same sink abstraction internally via ParquetSink

Use the sink registry for named sink creation:

from boti_data import SinkPipeline, available_sinks

assert "jsonl" in available_sinks()

pipeline = SinkPipeline(
    helper,
    "jsonl",
    sink_config={
        "storage_path": "/tmp/source_events_jsonl",
        "partition_on": ["partition_date"],
    },
    date_field="event_date",
)
result = pipeline.write(filters={"status__exact": "active"})

from boti_data import CsvSink, DataHelper, SinkPipeline

helper = DataHelper(
    backend="sqlalchemy",
    connection_url=f"sqlite:///{db_path}",
    poolclass="sqlalchemy.pool.NullPool",
    query_only=False,
    table="source_events",
)

sink = CsvSink(
    {
        "storage_path": "/tmp/source_events_csv",
        "partition_on": ["partition_date"],
    }
)

pipeline = SinkPipeline(helper, sink, date_field="event_date")
result = pipeline.write(filters={"status__exact": "active"})

assert result.files

CsvSink/JsonlSink are intentionally write-only in this release. Use ParquetPipeline when you need write + reload orchestration. See examples/data_csv_sink_pipeline.py and examples/data_jsonl_sink_pipeline.py for runnable examples.

docs.title: Enrichment v1
docs.text:
AsyncFrameEnricher adds declarative attachment-based enrichment before downstream writes. Select attachments by AttachmentSpec.key via cols=[...], and enforce bounded unique-value extraction with max_unique_values.

from boti_data import AsyncFrameEnricher, AttachmentSpec

enricher = AsyncFrameEnricher(
    [
        AttachmentSpec(
            key="customer_segment",
            required_cols={"customer_id"},
            attachment_fn=customer_segment_attachment,
            col_to_kwarg={"customer_id": "ids"},
            left_on=["customer_id"],
            right_on=["id"],
            drop_cols=["id"],
            max_unique_values=5000,
        )
    ]
)
enriched = await enricher.aenrich(base_frame, cols=["customer_segment"])

SinkPipeline accepts enricher=... and optional enrich_cols=[...] to apply enrichment right before sink writes.

docs.title: SQL loads
docs.text: Everything that reads rows from a SQL database: the single-row repositories, the low-level resource, and DataHelper/DataGateway for dataframes. Driver installation and the backend-specific notes for ClickHouse, DuckDB and pgvector are in Installation.

docs.title: DataHelper
docs.text: DataHelper is the primary entry point for most use cases. It is a thin facade over DataGateway that provides a clean, consistent interface for loading data whether you are working locally, in a notebook, or inside a distributed Dask pipeline.

docs.title: Creating a DataHelper
docs.text:
DataHelper accepts a DataGateway, a backend config object, or a plain dict:

from boti_data import DataHelper, SqlDatabaseConfig

# From a config object
config = SqlDatabaseConfig(
    connection_url="mysql+pymysql://user:pass@host/mydb",
    query_only=True,
)
helper = DataHelper(config, table="orders")

# From a dict (useful for config-driven setups)
helper = DataHelper({
    "backend": "sqlalchemy",
    "connection_url": "mysql+pymysql://user:pass@host/mydb",
    "table": "orders",
    "query_only": True,
})

# From keyword arguments
helper = DataHelper(
    backend="sqlalchemy",
    connection_url="mysql+pymysql://user:pass@host/mydb",
    table="orders",
)

Using DataHelper as a context manager ensures connections are properly closed:

with DataHelper(config, table="orders") as helper:
    df = helper.load(status="confirmed")

Async context managers are also supported:

async with DataHelper(config, table="orders") as helper:
    df = await helper.aload(status="confirmed")

For synchronous scripts that still need to call async load paths, use the explicit sync bridge:

with DataHelper(config, table="orders") as helper:
    df = helper.aload_sync(status="confirmed")

If an event loop is already running (for example notebooks or ASGI handlers), use await helper.aload(...) directly.

docs.title: Output engines: pandas, polars, and dask
docs.text:
DataHelper exposes three engine-bound views that pin the output type for a call chain:

helper = DataHelper(config, table="orders")

# Always returns pandas.DataFrame
df = helper.pandas.load(status="confirmed")

# Always returns polars.DataFrame
df = helper.polars.load(status="confirmed")

# Always returns dask.dataframe.DataFrame (lazy)
df = helper.dask.load(status="confirmed")

These are the cleanest way to use a single helper across different downstream contexts. You can also pass return_type explicitly to load or aload when you need more control:

# Explicit return_type on a single call
df = helper.load(status="confirmed", return_type="polars")
df = helper.load(status="confirmed", return_type="pandas")
df = helper.load(status="confirmed", return_type="dask")
df = helper.load(status="confirmed", return_type="arrow")  # pyarrow.Table

docs.title: Choosing an output engine
docs.text:
Engine Type returned Best for pandas pandas.DataFrame Small-to-medium data, notebooks, local analysis polars polars.DataFrame CPU-intensive transforms, single-machine performance arrow pyarrow.Table Zero-copy interchange, serialisation, ML pipelines dask dask.dataframe.DataFrame Large datasets, distributed clusters, lazy evaluation auto decided at runtime Unknown result size; boti-data uses backend-aware size heuristics

return_type="auto" uses pandas for small results and switches to Dask for larger scans, with backend-specific checks:

  • SQL: probes up to 10,000 rows (and respects limit / explicit partitioned controls).
  • Parquet: uses pandas when the selected scan is small enough to estimate eagerly (typically up to 4 files and <= 32 MB total), otherwise Dask.

Use auto when result size is uncertain and you want sensible defaults without hardcoding an engine.

docs.title: Streaming a result
docs.text:
iter_batches never materialises the whole result. SQL sources read through a server-side cursor, Parquet sources through dataset batches, and each batch is a typed pyarrow.RecordBatch already renamed through the gateway's field map:

with DataGateway(config, table="orders") as gateway:
    for batch in gateway.iter_batches(status="active", batch_size=50_000):
        sink.write(batch)          # about one batch of memory at any time

with SqlRepository(config, "orders") as repo:
    for batch in repo.iter_batches(columns=["id", "total"]):
        ...

return_type="polars" builds the frame from Arrow directly (no pandas on the way), and return_type="arrow" needs no engine extra at all.

With boti-data[adbc] installed, read-only partition fetches on PostgreSQL and SQLite use the ADBC driver and skip DBAPI rows entirely; see installation for the guards that keep that path read-only.

docs.title: Non-distributed usage
docs.text:
For local analysis, notebooks, or small-scale pipelines, use DataHelper without any Dask cluster. The default output is a Dask DataFrame, but you can force pandas or polars.

from boti_data import DataHelper, SqlDatabaseConfig

config = SqlDatabaseConfig(
    connection_url="sqlite:///local.db",
    query_only=True,
)

with DataHelper(config, table="orders") as helper:
    # Pandas — eager, in-memory
    df = helper.pandas.load(status="shipped")

    # Polars — eager, high-performance single-machine
    df = helper.polars.load(status="shipped")

    # Date range load with pandas output
    df = helper.pandas.load_period("created_at", "2024-01-01", "2024-03-31")

For async contexts (FastAPI, async services):

async def get_orders(status: str) -> pd.DataFrame:
    async with DataHelper(config, table="orders") as helper:
        return await helper.pandas.aload(status=status)

docs.title: Repository (lightest-weight, no dataframe dependencies)
docs.text:
For single-row transactional access — get/insert/update/delete by primary key — without pulling in dask/pandas/polars at all. Rows come back as plain dict[str, Any], never a DataFrame.

query_only defaults to True on SqlRepository/AsyncSqlRepository themselves and always wins over whatever the passed-in config.query_only says — insert/update/delete raise until you opt in explicitly with query_only=False. This is deliberate: a config object might be shared with or reused from a context where writes are already enabled, and a repository shouldn't silently inherit write access nobody asked it for.

from boti_data import SqlDatabaseConfig, SqlRepository

config = SqlDatabaseConfig(connection_url="sqlite:///example.db")

with SqlRepository(config, "users", query_only=False) as users:
    row = users.insert({"id": 1, "name": "Ada"})
    row = users.get(1)              # -> dict | None
    row = users.update(1, {"name": "Grace"})
    deleted = users.delete(1)       # -> bool

Omit query_only=False (or read-only access is all you need) and writes raise instead of silently succeeding:

with SqlRepository(config, "users") as users:
    users.get(1)                    # fine
    users.insert({"id": 2, "name": "Bob"})  # raises SQLAlchemyError

An async counterpart, AsyncSqlRepository, mirrors the same four methods as coroutines and is used as an async context manager:

from boti_data import AsyncSqlRepository

async with AsyncSqlRepository(config, "users", query_only=False) as users:
    row = await users.get(1)

docs.title: Multi-table atomic transactions
docs.text:
By default each SqlRepository owns its own connection and commits after every write — fine for independent single-row operations, but not when several writes (potentially across different tables) need to succeed or fail together. Pass an already-open session instead of config to bind a repository to a transaction you control; writes flush() instead of committing, so nothing is durable until you commit the session yourself:

with SqlDatabaseResource(config) as db, db.session() as session:
    with SqlRepository(session=session, table_name="audit_log") as audit_log:
        with SqlRepository(session=session, table_name="embeddings") as embeddings:
            audit_log.insert({"event": "enroll"})
            embeddings.insert({"subject_id": 1, "vector": [...]})
    session.commit()  # both rows commit together, or neither does on an exception

SqlUnitOfWork wraps this pattern for the common case — one config, several tables, one commit/rollback:

from boti_data import SqlDatabaseConfig, SqlUnitOfWork

config = SqlDatabaseConfig(connection_url="postgresql+psycopg://user:pass@host/mydb")

with SqlUnitOfWork(config, query_only=False) as uow:
    uow.repository("audit_log").insert({"event": "enroll"})
    uow.repository("embeddings").insert({"subject_id": 1, "vector": [...]})
# commits both on clean exit; rolls back both on any exception

query_only on a session-bound SqlRepository is inert — the session's own class (e.g. a ReadOnlySession) already determines writability, since this path never builds a new guarded session itself. AsyncSqlUnitOfWork mirrors SqlUnitOfWork, with an async repository() method (returns an already-set-up AsyncSqlRepository, so callers don't need to async with each one individually):

from boti_data import AsyncSqlUnitOfWork

async with AsyncSqlUnitOfWork(config, query_only=False) as uow:
    audit_log = await uow.repository("audit_log")
    embeddings = await uow.repository("embeddings")
    await audit_log.insert({"event": "enroll"})
    await embeddings.insert({"subject_id": 1, "vector": [...]})

docs.title: Nearest-neighbour search (pgvector)
docs.text:
boti_data.db.nearest_neighbors/vector_distance build an ORDER BY <distance> LIMIT k statement against a pgvector column, with the query vector bound as a driver parameter — never string-interpolated into the SQL, regardless of how large the vector is. Requires boti-data[pgvector] (see Installation) and a table reflected via SqlAlchemyModelBuilder/SqlRepository/DataGateway.

from boti_data import DataGateway, SqlDatabaseConfig
from boti_data.db import SqlAlchemyModelBuilder, nearest_neighbors

config = SqlDatabaseConfig(connection_url="postgresql+psycopg://user:pass@host/mydb", query_only=True)
gateway = DataGateway(config)

model = SqlAlchemyModelBuilder(gateway.resource.engine, "embeddings").build_model()
query_vector = [...]  # e.g. a 512-float face embedding

stmt = nearest_neighbors(model, model.vector, query_vector, k=10, metric="cosine")
matches = gateway.load(statement=stmt, model=model, as_pandas=True)

Supported metric values map directly to pgvector's operators: "cosine" (<=>), "l2" (<->), "inner_product" (<#>), "l1" (<+>). Add ordinary filtering with .where(...) on the statement before passing it to gateway.load(...).

docs.title: Raw sql= safety policy (eager SQL only)
docs.text:
DataGateway supports convenience sql="..." reads for eager SQL paths, with explicit safety controls:

  • raw SQL is validated as read-only single-statement SELECT/WITH
  • mutating SQL (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, DROP, etc.) is rejected
  • multi-statement SQL is rejected
  • lazy SQL still requires statement + model (raw sql= is eager-only)

Use constructor policy raw_sql_policy to control availability:

  • raw_sql_policy="readonly_opt_in" (default): call site must pass allow_raw_sql=True
  • raw_sql_policy="disabled": raw sql= is blocked even if allow_raw_sql=True
from boti_data import DataGateway, SqlDatabaseConfig

config = SqlDatabaseConfig(connection_url="sqlite:///example.db", query_only=True)

with DataGateway(config, raw_sql_policy="readonly_opt_in") as gateway:
    df = gateway.load(
        sql="SELECT id, status FROM users WHERE status = :status",
        params={"status": "active"},
        as_pandas=True,
        allow_raw_sql=True,
    )

Prefer statement + model for production query paths whenever possible, especially when you need lazy/partitioned execution.

docs.title: Metrics and tracing
docs.text: boti-data emits spans and metrics through one process-wide provider, chosen by a single setting. By default nothing is recorded and the cost is one attribute lookup per instrumented call. The boti Logger stays the log sink; telemetry adds signals alongside the existing diagnostics=True log lines, it does not replace them.

docs.title: Choosing a provider
docs.text:
from boti_data import telemetry

telemetry.configure(telemetry.OpenTelemetryProvider())   # needs boti-data[otel]
telemetry.configure(telemetry.InMemoryProvider())        # tests and diagnostics
telemetry.configure(None)                                # back to the no-op

Or from the environment, read on first use: BOTI_DATA_TELEMETRY=otel (none is the default). telemetry.current_provider() returns the active one.

OpenTelemetryProvider uses the tracer and meter providers the application configured globally and never installs exporters itself, so one OpenTelemetry setup serves boti-data and boti-dask alike.

docs.title: What is emitted
docs.text:
Instrument Name Attributes span boti_data.load backend, return_type, execution_mode, rows when materialised span boti_data.partitioned.load gate span boti_data.partition.fetch gate, partition when known, rows histogram boti_data.gate.wait_seconds gate counter boti_data.pool.checkouts engine gauge boti_data.pool.checked_out engine

gate is the hash of the engine identity that names the cluster-wide fetch gate; engine is the sixteen-character digest of the connection URL. Neither ever carries the DSN or its credentials.

Pool instruments come from SQLAlchemy's PoolEvents on every engine boti-data builds: the resource engines behind SqlDatabaseResource, the async engines (through sync_engine) and the worker-local engines partition fetches use. The gate histogram records every wait for a fetch slot, the same observations that feed fetch_gate_stats().

docs.title: Prometheus
docs.text:
Point the OpenTelemetry SDK at a Prometheus reader once at service start-up; boti-data then reports through it without further configuration:

from opentelemetry import metrics
from opentelemetry.exporter.prometheus import PrometheusMetricReader
from opentelemetry.sdk.metrics import MeterProvider
from prometheus_client import start_http_server

from boti_data import telemetry

start_http_server(9464)
metrics.set_meter_provider(MeterProvider(metric_readers=[PrometheusMetricReader()]))
telemetry.configure(telemetry.OpenTelemetryProvider())

A scrape of :9464/metrics then shows boti_data_pool_checked_out, boti_data_pool_checkouts_total and boti_data_gate_wait_seconds_bucket, which is what to alert on for pool exhaustion and gate contention. Traces go wherever the global tracer provider exports them (an OTLP exporter, for instance); install it the same way before configuring the provider.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text: InMemoryProvider keeps every span and observation in memory, with spans_named(), total() and last() helpers, so a test can assert on exactly what a load emitted without any SDK installed.

docs.title: Big-data readiness
docs.text: Boti is ready for Dask-first large workloads today, with some clear boundaries.

docs.title: Recommended operating model
docs.text:
1. Use return_type="dask" for large reads.
  2. Run under an explicit Dask client or dask_session(...).
  3. Prefer partitioned SQL reads or parquet-backed datasets.
  4. Prune columns and push filters down as early as possible.
  5. Use indexed_left_join(...) for large distributed joins after aligning join-key dtypes.
  6. Persist after expensive repartition/index boundaries when the result will be reused.
  7. Materialize only at the edge for exports, samples, or compact aggregates.
  8. Use resilient=True when you want Dask persistence to go through the resilience layer.
  9. Use apply_recommended_dask_config(...) for shuffle-heavy workloads.

docs.title: What Boti already supports
docs.text:
• partitioned SQL loading through DataGateway and SqlPartitionedLoader
  • lazy Dask execution on local or external distributed schedulers
  • explicit session ownership via DaskSession / dask_session(...)
  • schema-aware distributed joins via indexed_left_join(...)
  • resilient Dask helpers for sync, async, and distributed actions
  • opt-in resilient indexed joins via indexed_left_join(..., resilient=True)
  • opt-in Dask config preset via apply_recommended_dask_config(...)
  • opt-in diagnostics on gateway loads and joins with diagnostics=True
  • eager result modes (pandas, arrow, polars) for small-result convenience

docs.title: What diagnostics=True gives you
docs.text:
For gateway loads:

  • requested vs resolved return type
  • active Dask client summary
  • partition plan summary
  • load timing and Dask graph/partition metrics

For joins:

  • active client summary
  • input/output frame metrics
  • timing for indexed joins
  • warning when a direct Dask merge is likely to trigger a large shuffle
  • warning when persist=False may cause repeated recomputation
  • graph metrics for lazy Dask gateway loads

docs.title: SQL-backed workloads
docs.text:
• Prefer file-backed or network-reachable databases for worker access.
  • Keep partitioned statements free of LIMIT, OFFSET, and ORDER BY; let the loader manage partition planning.
  • Choose explicit partition_column / order_column when defaults are not ideal.

docs.title: Parquet-backed workloads
docs.text:
• Prefer parquet for repeated large analytics and intermediate datasets.
  • Organize data so partition pruning is meaningful.
  • Use filesystem profiles or project-rooted paths that are visible to the workers.

docs.title: Join-heavy workloads
docs.text:
• Normalize join-key dtypes before joining.
  • For large joins, set indexes on the join key and join on the index.
  • Persist after set_index(...) if downstream work will reuse the result.
  • Prefer resilient=True for long-running or remote distributed joins.

docs.title: Readiness status
docs.text:
Ready now

  • local distributed development
  • explicit remote-style scheduler attachment
  • partitioned SQL + parquet lazy loading
  • indexed distributed joins
  • basic diagnostics and workload visibility
  • resilience helpers for compute/persist/wait/inspection
  • recommended opt-in config profile for shuffle-heavy jobs

Still maturing

  • broader validation against real remote clusters and object stores
  • heavier benchmark coverage for skew, spill, and failure scenarios
  • more production cookbook material for deployment-specific tuning

docs.title: Minimal example
docs.text:
from dask.distributed import LocalCluster
from sqlalchemy import select

from boti_data import (
    DataGateway,
    SqlDatabaseConfig,
    apply_recommended_dask_config,
    dask_session,
    indexed_left_join,
)

config = SqlDatabaseConfig(connection_url="sqlite:///warehouse.db", query_only=False)

with apply_recommended_dask_config():
    with LocalCluster(n_workers=2, threads_per_worker=1, processes=False, dashboard_address=":0") as cluster:
        with dask_session(scheduler_address=cluster.scheduler_address):
            with DataGateway(config) as gateway:
                left = gateway.load(
                    statement=select(User),
                    model=User,
                    persist=True,
                    resilient=True,
                    diagnostics=True,
                )
                right = gateway.load(
                    statement=select(UserProfile),
                    model=UserProfile,
                    persist=True,
                    resilient=True,
                    diagnostics=True,
                )
                joined = indexed_left_join(
                    left,
                    right,
                    join_key="id",
                    join_schema_map={"id": "Int64"},
                    persist=True,
                    resilient=True,
                    diagnostics=True,
                )
                result = joined.head()

docs.title: Dask resilience and cluster-lifecycle use cases for boti-data
Summary
docs.text:
Reviewing sibi_flux.dask_cluster and sibi_dst.utils.dask_resilience shows a consistent theme: both packages add a resilience layer above ordinary Dask usage rather than replacing Dask itself. The main ideas are:

  • keep a healthy client available
  • retry on recoverable comm failures
  • avoid unsafe fallback for Dask DataFrame graphs
  • expose graph and cluster diagnostics
  • optionally share or heal cluster state across processes

boti-data now relies on boti_dask for this runtime foundation:

  • ../boti-dask/src/boti_dask/session.py for explicit client/session ownership
  • ../boti-dask/src/boti_dask/resilience.py for resilient wrappers and emptiness helpers
  • ../boti-dask/src/boti_dask/diagnostics.py for graph/frame diagnostics
  • src/boti_data/gateway/core.py for load diagnostics and client summaries
  • src/boti_data/joins.py for diagnostics around large distributed joins
  • src/boti_data/db/partitioned_loader.py for worker-safe partitioned SQL loading

That means the best opportunity is selective adoption: add resilience and observability around high-value distributed operations without importing the full lifecycle model from the reviewed projects.

docs.title: sibi_flux.dask_cluster
docs.text:
Most relevant patterns:

  • persistent/shared client registry via a temp-file registry and refcounting
  • connectivity verification before accepting a scheduler/client as healthy
  • watchdog-based healing when scheduler comms fail
  • safe compute/persist/gather wrappers with one retry after client rebind
  • strict invariant: never silently fall back to local threaded compute for Dask DataFrame/Series graphs
  • graph inspection / dry run to log task count, layers, and partition counts before execution
  • optional local code deployment to workers for remote scheduler scenarios

This module is the stronger reference for cluster lifecycle and operational safety.

docs.title: sibi_dst.utils.dask_resilience
docs.text:
Most relevant patterns:

  • global Dask config hardening, especially dataframe.shuffle.method = "tasks"
  • narrower recoverable exception policy
  • sync and async safe wrappers for compute/persist/gather/wait
  • cheap emptiness probes for Dask collections
  • resilient unique value extraction

This module is the stronger reference for execution wrappers and defensive data utilities.

docs.title: Current boti-data baseline
docs.text:
boti-data already supports (directly or through boti_dask):

  • explicit DaskSession / dask_session(...)
  • local or remote scheduler attachment
  • diagnostics for gateway loads and joins
  • partitioned SQL execution designed for worker-local engines
  • Dask-first joins through indexed_left_join(...)

What it does not currently provide:

  • automatic client healing or rebind-and-retry
  • resilient wrappers around expensive distributed actions
  • persistent shared-cluster reuse across notebook/process boundaries
  • explicit dry-run graph inspection before large actions
  • Dask-specific helpers like resilient emptiness/unique-value probes

docs.title: 1. Resilient materialization of expensive Dask loads
Problem
docs.text:
Large DataGateway.load(..., return_type="dask") workloads often end in a small number of materialization points:

  • .persist() after repartition or indexing
  • .compute() for exports or model inputs
  • .head() / sample extraction for notebook inspection

If the client drops during these steps, users currently have to manage recovery themselves.

docs.title: Use case
docs.text:
Add opt-in helpers such as:

  • safe_compute(frame, client=None, logger=None)
  • safe_persist(frame, client=None, logger=None)
  • safe_wait(obj, client=None, timeout=None)

These should:

  1. detect an active client
  2. retry once on recoverable comm failures
  3. refuse unsafe local fallback for Dask DataFrames
  4. surface a clear error instructing the caller to rebuild the collection when the graph is orphaned

docs.text: indexed_left_join(...) already recommends persist=True for expensive join pipelines, but the actual persist step is still a plain Dask action. If a cluster hiccup happens after set_index(...), the user may face recomputation or ambiguous failures.

docs.title: Use case

Wrap the expensive boundary operations used by distributed joins:

Problem
docs.text: boti-data already logs frame summaries after work is planned or completed, but it does not provide a first-class way to inspect graph size before execution.

docs.title: Use case
docs.text:
Add an optional dry-run / inspection helper for Dask-backed frames that logs:

  • number of partitions
  • number of graph layers

docs.title: 4. Shared cluster/session reuse in notebook and ETL workflows
Problem
docs.text: boti-data has explicit session ownership, which is clean and predictable, but repeated notebook cells or multi-step ETL scripts may repeatedly reconnect or recreate clients.

docs.title: Use case
docs.text:
Introduce an optional shared-session mode on top of DaskSession, for example:

  • reuse the current context client if one exists
  • otherwise attach to a configured scheduler address
  • optionally keep a process-local singleton client for repeated operations

This does not require the full file-registry model from sibi_flux on day one.

docs.title: 5. Defensive Dask defaults for shuffle-heavy pipelines
Problem
docs.text: The reviewed modules explicitly harden Dask config for comm timeouts, memory spill thresholds, and shuffle behavior. boti-data currently leaves these concerns largely to caller environment and cluster configuration.

docs.title: Use case
docs.text:
Provide a documented or opt-in config profile for large distributed boti-data workloads, especially:

  • dataframe.shuffle.method = "tasks"
  • conservative comm timeout defaults
  • memory spill / pause thresholds
  • large-graph warning thresholds

This is especially relevant for:

  • indexed_left_join(...)
  • partitioned SQL loads feeding downstream joins
  • large parquet scans followed by repartition or groupby

docs.text: Medium-high. Likely the simplest way to reduce operational failures without invasive code changes.

docs.title: Problem
docs.text:
Big Dask frames are often probed for:

  • “is this empty?”
  • “give me representative unique values”
  • “can I cheaply inspect a few results before computing all of it?”

Naive implementations can be either too expensive or fragile.

docs.title: Use case
docs.text:
Add small utilities such as:

  • dask_is_probably_empty(frame)
  • dask_is_empty(frame, sample=4, client=None)
  • extract_unique_values(frame, *columns, limit=...)

These would be useful in:

  • UI/data validation layers built on top of DataHelper
  • diagnostics notebooks
  • data quality checks before exporting or joining

docs.text: • ../boti-dask/src/boti_dask/resilience.py

docs.title: Value
docs.text: Medium. Useful, but secondary to resilient compute/persist/wait.

docs.title: 7. Remote-cluster bootstrap and worker code deployment
Problem
docs.text: sibi_flux includes automatic package zip/upload to workers and registry-driven cluster healing. That is useful when workers do not automatically have the same Python package available.

docs.title: Use case in boti-data
docs.text: Limited. boti-data is primarily a library, and worker environment packaging is usually better solved through deployment tooling, container images, or environment management rather than runtime zip upload.

docs.title: Value
docs.text: Low for near-term adoption. This is probably not the first place to invest.

docs.title: Recommended adoption order
docs.text: Priority Candidate Why it fits boti-data 1 resilient compute/persist/wait wrappers protects the most expensive distributed actions with minimal API surface 2 join-boundary resilience directly improves indexed_left_join(...) workflows 3 dry-run graph inspection complements existing diagnostics cleanly 4 opt-in Dask config profile low-cost operational improvement 5 emptiness/unique-value helpers useful utilities for notebook and validation workflows 6 shared singleton session mode helpful, but should stay optional 7 registry/watchdog + code deployment operationally heavier than current repo needs

docs.title: Prefer wrappers over automatic magic
docs.text:
The reviewed packages are comfortable with hidden healing and shared global state. boti-data currently favors more explicit control. The best fit is:

  • explicit session ownership by default
  • opt-in resilience helpers
  • strong diagnostics when healing or retry happens
  • no silent fallback from distributed DataFrame graphs to local execution

docs.title: Keep DataFrame safety as an invariant
docs.text:
One of the best ideas in both reviewed modules is the rule:

if a Dask DataFrame graph loses its client or worker dependencies, do not pretend local compute is a safe fallback.

That rule aligns well with boti-data’s big-data positioning and should be preserved if resilience helpers are added.

docs.title: Reuse existing diagnostics surface
docs.text:
boti-data already has:

  • current_client_summary()
  • describe_frame(...)
  • gateway load diagnostics
  • join diagnostics

New resilience features should plug into that existing logging model instead of creating a parallel system.

docs.title: Concrete near-term proposal
docs.text:
The first increment was implemented in boti_dask, which now provides:

  1. safe_compute
  2. safe_persist
  3. safe_wait
  4. inspect_graph
  5. an opt-in Dask config helper for large shuffles

Then wire those helpers into:

  • indexed_left_join(..., persist=True, diagnostics=True)
  • large DataGateway distributed loads when diagnostics=True
  • examples and docs for notebook / ETL usage

This would capture most of the practical value from the reviewed modules without importing the heaviest parts of their lifecycle model.

docs.title: Final assessment
docs.text:
The reviewed modules are relevant to boti-data, but not as a direct transplant.

The strongest boti-data use cases are:

  • resilient compute/persist/wait around large Dask frames
  • safer distributed join workflows
  • graph inspection before expensive execution
  • documented Dask hardening defaults for shuffle-heavy analytics

The weakest use cases are:

  • full registry-based cluster lifecycle management
  • automatic worker code deployment

In short, boti-data should borrow the execution-safety and observability ideas first, while keeping cluster ownership explicit and lightweight.

docs.title: Datacube Contract
docs.text: boti-data supports callable-backed datacube loading through DatacubeConfig. Use DatacubeContract when you want typed request hooks and centralized validation.

docs.title: Contract Hooks
docs.text:
DatacubeContract supports these optional hooks:

  • request_transformer(request) -> request
  • request_validator(request) -> None
  • loader(request) -> frame
  • async_loader(request) -> awaitable[frame]
  • frame_transformer(frame, request) -> frame

Supported frame outputs are:

  • pandas.DataFrame
  • dask.dataframe.DataFrame
  • pyarrow.Table
  • polars.DataFrame

docs.title: Execution Order
docs.text:
At runtime, DatacubeResource applies hooks in this order:

  1. apply default_cube when request has no explicit cube
  2. run request_transformer (if set)
  3. run request_validator (if set)
  4. execute loader (contract.async_loader / contract.loader first, then config loaders)
  5. run frame_transformer (if set)

Loader precedence:

  • sync path: contract.loader -> DatacubeConfig.loader
  • async path: contract.async_loader -> DatacubeConfig.async_loader -> sync fallback in thread

docs.title: Validation Failures
docs.text:
If request_validator raises, boti-data surfaces an actionable error message with request context:

  • selected cube
  • list of filter keys
  • guidance to fix validator inputs or validator logic

Example message shape:

Datacube contract request validation failed: cube must be 'orders'. Request context cube='inventory', filter_keys=['status__exact']. Adjust DatacubeContract.request_validator or pass valid cube/filter inputs.

For end-to-end SQL/datacube defensive defaults, see docs/SECURITY_HARDENING.md.

docs.title: Minimal Pattern
docs.text:
import pandas as pd

from boti_data import DatacubeConfig, DatacubeContract, DataGateway


def loader(request):
    return pd.DataFrame({"id": [1], "status": ["active"]})


def validator(request):
    if request.cube != "orders":
        raise ValueError("cube must be 'orders'")


contract = DatacubeContract(
    loader=loader,
    request_validator=validator,
    request_transformer=lambda request: request.model_copy(
        update={"cube": request.cube or "orders"}
    ),
)

with DataGateway(DatacubeConfig(contract=contract)) as gateway:
    frame = gateway.load(return_type="pandas", status__exact="active")

docs.title: Findings
docs.text:
1. For eager/pandas paths, chunking is a major regression once IN grows:
  2. IN=10,000: sync_pandas_auto_chunk is ~7x slower than single-query.
  3. Similar degradation on async eager (async_pandas_auto_chunk).
  4. For lazy/dask paths, chunking helps at larger cardinalities:
  5. IN=10,000: sync_dask_auto_chunk is ~2.6x faster than single-query.
  6. Current auto threshold (~900) is too low for eager paths on this backend.
  7. The same chunk policy is being applied without enough sensitivity to:
  8. execution mode (eager vs lazy)
  9. backend/dialect characteristics
  10. crossover point where chunk fan-out starts paying off.

docs.title: Phase 1: Low-Risk Tuning (recommended first)
docs.text:
1. Make auto chunking execution-mode aware in DataGateway:
  2. For eager paths (pandas/polars):
    • default to in_chunk_strategy="off" unless IN is very large.
  3. For lazy/dask paths:
    • keep chunking enabled.
  4. Raise eager auto chunk activation threshold (dialect-specific):
  5. SQLite baseline suggestion: do not auto-chunk until at least IN >= 8,000.
  6. Cap eager chunk concurrency at 1 by default:
  7. Avoid thread fan-out overhead for local DB workloads.

Expected impact:

  • Substantial latency reduction for large eager IN filters (4x-7x in baseline patterns).

docs.text:
1. Introduce a backend/dialect policy object, e.g.:
  2. sqlite: high eager threshold, lower concurrency
  3. postgres/mysql: threshold tuned from backend benchmarks
  4. Add crossover telemetry in diagnostics logs:
  5. chunk count
  6. per-chunk elapsed
  7. total fan-out overhead

Expected impact:

  • Better default behavior across environments without manual tuning.

docs.text:
For very large lists (e.g., >20k to 50k, backend-dependent), evaluate:

  1. temporary table + join
  2. backend-native array strategies (where supported)

Expected impact:

  • Improved plan stability and lower SQL/parameter overhead for extreme cardinalities.

docs.title: Rollout Plan
docs.text:
1. Implement Phase 1 tuning behind safe defaults.
  2. Re-run benchmark matrix and compare to this baseline.
  3. Add regression benchmarks to CI-adjacent perf checks (non-blocking initially).
  4. Progress to Phase 2 after validating no regressions in distributed/lazy paths.

docs.text:
For the same baseline harness:

  • sync_pandas_auto_chunk at IN=5,000 and IN=10,000 should be within 1.5x of sync_pandas_single (or better).
  • sync_dask_auto_chunk should not regress at IN=5,000 and IN=10,000.
  • No correctness deltas in returned row counts.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• These numbers are from a local SQLite benchmark and are intended as a baseline.
  • Final tuning should be validated against your production DB engine and network profile.

docs.title: PyArrow Integration Proposal — Enhancing Boti Performance
Executive Summary
docs.text:
Boti currently uses PyArrow only for filesystem I/O and parquet dataset discovery. All in-memory data flows through pandas/Dask, missing significant performance opportunities. This proposal outlines a phased integration strategy to leverage PyArrow's zero-copy reads, vectorized compute kernels, and batch coercion across critical performance paths.

Expected impact: 2–10x speedup on partitioned SQL loads, 5–50x on string filter operations, and 3–5x on schema coercion pipelines.

docs.title: Where PyArrow Is Used Today
docs.text: Module Usage Limitation parquet/resource.py pyarrow.dataset for file discovery & partitioning Only extracts file paths; data read goes to Dask/pandas core/filesystem.py pyarrow.fs for Local/S3 filesystem bridges Used as a passthrough, not for compute data/schema.py PyArrow dtype string aliases ("int64[pyarrow]") Normalization only; no actual Arrow types core/connection_catalog.py Type hints for pyarrow.fs.FileSystem Type annotation only

docs.title: The Core Problem
docs.text:
Parquet Path:  Parquet → PyArrow (internal to Dask) → pandas partitions → Dask graph
SQL Path:      SQLAlchemy cursor → pd.DataFrame(rows) → apply_schema_map() → Dask

Data never materializes as a PyArrow Table in application code. Every operation — filtering, coercion, sorting, aggregation — goes through pandas, which means: - Row-by-row pandas construction from SQLAlchemy cursors (slow for large partitions) - Per-column coercion loops via pd.to_datetime(), pd.to_numeric(), .astype() - String operations via pandas .str.* methods (not vectorized) - No zero-copy concatenation for chunked IN-list results

docs.title: Phase 1: Arrow-Backed SQL Partition Loading (Highest Impact)
docs.text:
Target: data/db/partitioned_execution.py, data/db/sql_model_builder.py

Current hot path (runs for every SQL partition): 

# partitioned_execution.py:86-101
frame = pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=columns)
return SqlPartitionExecutor.align_and_coerce_partition(frame, meta_dtypes)

Proposed change: 

import pyarrow as pa

# Build Arrow Arrays directly from column buffers (zero-copy from driver where supported)
arrays = [pa.array([row[i] for row in rows], type=arrow_type) for i, arrow_type in enumerate(arrow_types)]
batch = pa.RecordBatch.from_arrays(arrays, names=columns)
table = pa.Table.from_batches([batch])

# Single-pass coercion instead of per-column loop
table = table.cast(target_arrow_schema)
return table.to_pandas(types_mapper=_get_dtype_mapper)  # or return Arrow directly

Benefits: - Eliminates per-row pandas DataFrame construction overhead - Replaces apply_schema_map() column-by-column loop with table.cast_to_schema() (single pass) - Estimated 2–5x speedup on large partition fetches

Implementation details: 1. Add data/db/arrow_schema_mapper.py — maps SQLAlchemy types to PyArrow types 2. Modify SqlPartitionExecutor.fetch_partition() to build Arrow batches 3. Add configuration flag use_arrow=True on DataGateway for opt-in migration 4. Maintain backward compatibility — fallback to pandas path when use_arrow=False

docs.title: Phase 2: Arrow Compute Kernels for Filter Operations
docs.text:
Target: data/filters/utils.py, data/filters/handler.py

Current limitations: - String operations (contains, startswith, regex) use pandas .str.* via map_partitions - $or/$not boolean operators excluded from pushdown — applied as residual pandas filters - Date casting in filters uses pd.Timestamp arithmetic

Proposed changes:

docs.title: 2a. Residual String Filters via PyArrow Compute
docs.text:
import pyarrow.compute as pc

# Current (slow):
column.map_partitions(lambda s: s.str.contains(pattern, na=False))

# Proposed (fast):
pc.match_substring(column_chunk, pattern=pattern)  # vectorized, zero-copy on Arrow chunk
pc.match_like(column_chunk, pattern)                # for LIKE patterns
pc.match_substring_regex(column_chunk, pattern)     # for regex

Implementation: 1. Add data/filters/arrow_kernels.py — PyArrow compute equivalents for all filter operations 2. Modify build_mask_fn() in handler.py to detect Arrow-backed columns and use pc.* kernels 3. Extend split_pushdown_and_residual() to include more operators in pushdown when Arrow is available

docs.title: 2b. $or/$not Boolean Operator Pushdown
docs.text:
# Current: $or returns empty pushdown, all applied as residual
# Proposed: Use PyArrow dataset expressions
import pyarrow.dataset as ds

ds.or_(filter_expr_a, filter_expr_b)
ds.invert(filter_expr)  # for $not

Benefits: - 5–50x speedup on string-heavy residual filters - Dramatically reduced memory usage (no intermediate pandas partitions for filtered data) - Better parquet pushdown coverage

docs.title: Phase 3: Arrow Schema as Canonical Contract
docs.text:
Target: data/schema.py, data/field_map.py

Current approach: 

# schema.py: dict-based dtype mapping + per-column coercion
SCHEMA_MAP = {"col_a": "Int64", "col_b": "boolean", "col_c": "datetime64[ns, UTC]"}
for col, dtype in schema_map.items():
    df[col] = _coerce_series(df[col], dtype)  # N separate passes

Proposed approach: 

# Define canonical PyArrow schema
ARROW_SCHEMA = pa.schema([
    ("col_a", pa.int64()),
    ("col_b", pa.bool_()),
    ("col_c", pa.timestamp("ns", tz="UTC")),
])

# Single-pass coercion
table = pa.Table.from_pandas(df)
table = table.cast(ARROW_SCHEMA)  # one operation, minimal copy

Implementation: 1. Add data/schema/arrow_schema.py — ArrowSchema class wrapping pa.Schema with: - from_dict() constructor from existing dict format - cast_table() method for single-pass coercion - equals() for validation (replaces validate_schema()) 2. Modify apply_schema_map() to use table.cast_to_schema() when Arrow is available 3. Add FieldMap.rename_table() — table.rename_columns() is O(1) (no data movement vs pandas rename)

Benefits: - 3–5x speedup on schema coercion (single pass vs N column loops) - Stronger schema contracts — pa.Schema has built-in equality, nullability, and metadata support - Cleaner dtype normalization — no more string alias parsing

docs.title: Phase 4: Arrow-Native DataGateway Path
docs.text:
Target: data/gateway/core.py, data/gateway/loaders.py

Current: DataGateway always returns pandas or Dask DataFrames.

Proposed: Add return_type parameter: "pandas" | "arrow" | "dask"

# New signature
gateway.load(
    query="...",
    return_type="arrow",  # new option
    filters={...},
)
# Returns: pa.Table (single partition) or list[pa.Table] (partitioned)

Data flow with Arrow path: 

SQL:     SQLAlchemy cursor → Arrow RecordBatch → pa.Table → (optional: to_pandas)
Parquet: pyarrow.dataset → pa.Table → (optional: to_dask / to_pandas)

Implementation: 1. Add return_type parameter to DataGateway.load(), load_all(), load_period(), semi_join(), etc. 2. Modify loaders (data/gateway/loaders.py) to produce Arrow Tables when requested 3. Add data/gateway/arrow_adapters.py — Arrow equivalents of Dask post-load transforms: - sort_by() via table.sort_by() - drop_duplicates() via table.group_by().aggregate() - concat_tables() via pa.concat_tables() (zero-copy) 4. Extend _apply_df_options() to _apply_table_options() for Arrow path

Benefits: - Users who don't need pandas can skip the conversion entirely - Downstream Arrow consumers (e.g., DuckDB, Polars, ML pipelines) get native input - Enables zero-copy interop with other Arrow-compatible libraries

docs.title: 5a. Parquet Statistics-Aware Partition Planning
docs.text:
Target: data/parquet/resource.py

Current file discovery only extracts paths. PyArrow datasets expose: - dataset.scanner().scan_statistics() — row counts, null counts, min/max per column - Fragment-level metadata — file sizes, row group info

Use cases: - Skip empty or irrelevant files before loading - Better partition sizing based on actual row counts - Predicate pushdown effectiveness estimation

docs.title: 5b. Arrow Memory-Mapped Reads for Large Parquet Files
docs.text:
import pyarrow.parquet as pq

# Current: full read into memory
table = pq.read_table(path)

# Proposed: memory-map for out-of-core processing
pf = pq.ParquetFile(path, memory_map=True)
table = pf.read_row_group(0)  # only needed row groups

docs.title: 5c. Dictionary Encoding for Categorical Columns
docs.text:
# Automatically dictionary-encode low-cardinality columns
table = table.combine_chunks()
table = table.replace_schema_metadata({"pandas_type": "categorical"})

Reduces memory footprint 5–20x for columns like status, country, type.

docs.title: 5d. IPC Serialization for Caching
docs.text:
# Arrow IPC format for fast intermediate caching
sink = pa.OSFile(path, "wb")
with pa.ipc.new_file(sink, table.schema) as writer:
    writer.write(table)

# Zero-copy read
with pa.ipc.open_file(path) as reader:
    table = reader.get_all()

Faster than parquet for write-once-read-many cached results.

docs.title: Implementation Roadmap
docs.text:
Phase Scope Estimated Effort Risk 1. Arrow SQL Loading partitioned_execution.py, new arrow_schema_mapper.py Medium Low — opt-in, backward compatible 2. Arrow Filter Kernels filters/utils.py, filters/handler.py, new arrow_kernels.py Medium Low — additive, no breaking changes 3. Arrow Schema Contract schema.py, field_map.py, new arrow_schema.py Low Low — wraps existing dict format 4. Arrow DataGateway Path gateway/core.py, loaders.py, new arrow_adapters.py High Medium — new API surface 5. Advanced Optimizations Statistics, memory-mapping, dictionary encoding, IPC Low each Low — optional features

Recommended order: Phase 1 → Phase 3 → Phase 2 → Phase 4 → Phase 5

Phase 1 gives the highest immediate ROI. Phase 3 strengthens the schema contract with minimal effort. Phase 2 builds on Phase 3's Arrow types. Phase 4 is the largest change but unlocks the full Arrow ecosystem.

docs.text: Risk Mitigation PyArrow version compatibility Pin minimum version (pyarrow>=14.0.0), test against multiple versions Memory overhead Arrow is columnar — large wide tables may use more memory; use chunked arrays and combine_chunks() judiciously Type mapping gaps Start with common types (int, float, string, bool, timestamp); add edge cases incrementally Breaking changes All Arrow features opt-in via use_arrow=False default; no existing behavior changes Dependency bloat PyArrow is already a dependency; no new external deps for Phases 1–3
